what-system-design-is.text: A stakeholder says "build me a URL shortener." You draw boxes for an hour and it falls apart in review because you never asked: how many redirects per second, how fresh must the click counts be, can a link ever 404 by mistake? System design is not box-drawing — it is converting an ambiguous ask into requirements and constraints that MAKE the tradeoffs for you. This lesson makes that conversion the first move, every time.

Every real design interview and every real design doc starts the same way: gather requirements, then let the numbers and constraints drive the architecture. Functional requirements say WHAT the system does (shorten a URL, redirect, count clicks). Non-functional requirements say HOW WELL (10k redirects/sec, p99 < 50ms, 99.99% available, counts may lag 1 min). Constraints (budget, a single region, a legal data-residency rule) are what turn "just add a cache" into a real decision. Skip this step and you optimize the wrong thing.

what-system-design-is.prompt: Before reading: for "design a URL shortener," write two functional requirements and two non-functional requirements. Which type usually decides the architecture?
what-system-design-is.reveal: Functional: create a short code for a long URL; redirect a short code to its long URL. Non-functional: handle N redirects/sec, redirect p99 latency < 50ms, 99.99% availability, click counts may be eventually consistent. The NON-FUNCTIONAL ones (scale, latency, availability, consistency freshness) decide the architecture — a shortener at 10 req/sec is a single box; at 100k req/sec it needs caching, sharding, and a CDN. Same functional spec, completely different system.

steps: Functional requirements are verbs the user performs — list them first, plainly.

what-system-design-is.commonMistake: Jumping to components ("we'll use Redis and Postgres") before writing the requirements. You end up defending tools instead of solving the stated problem, and you cannot justify a single choice because there is no number or constraint behind it.

what-system-design-is.text: System design is the discipline of turning an ambiguous product ask into a defensible architecture, and it always begins with three lists. FUNCTIONAL requirements are what the system must DO — the user-visible verbs (shorten, redirect, count). NON-FUNCTIONAL requirements are how well it must do them, and they are always numeric: throughput (requests/sec), latency at a percentile (p99 < 50ms, not "fast"), availability (99.9% vs 99.99%), durability, and consistency freshness (strong vs eventual). CONSTRAINTS are the immovable boundaries: budget, one region, a data-residency law, a fixed team size. The reason you gather these first is that the architecture is DERIVED from them, not chosen from taste: a requirement of 50 req/sec and one of 500k req/sec produce completely different systems from the identical functional spec. And the single most useful move is to find where two requirements CONFLICT under a constraint — "always fast redirects" (favor a cache) versus "never lose a click count" (favor durable writes) — because that tension is exactly what the rest of the course teaches you to resolve. If a domain expert reads your design and cannot find the driving numbers and the central tension, you have drawn boxes, not designed a system.
what-system-design-is.title: A design problem is requirements plus the constraint that makes them fight

storyboard.say: Everything starts with a raw ask like 'build me a URL shortener' — ambiguous, and useless as a blueprint until you interrogate it.
First, extract the verbs: what must the system do? Shorten a URL, redirect, count clicks — those are the functional requirements.
Then extract the numbers: ten thousand redirects per second, p99 under fifty milliseconds, four nines — how well it must do it, always numeric.
Those numbers are bounded by immovable constraints — budget, a single region, data-residency law, the size of your team.
Where the functional needs collide with the constraints, you find the driving tradeoff — the one tension this design must resolve.
The architecture is then derived from that tradeoff, not chosen from a catalog — which is why it survives review instead of falling apart.

back-of-envelope.proof: A capacity estimator that computes average and peak RPS, yearly storage, and peak bandwidth from a handful of product numbers.
back-of-envelope.unlock: You can size a system in under two minutes and defend each number, including the peak factor.
back-of-envelope.outcome: Estimate a system's load and footprint from first principles: DAU × actions → average RPS → peak RPS, and bytes/record → storage/year and bandwidth.
back-of-envelope.doNotClaim: Don't claim a system "scales" without a number — scale is the estimate that says single-box or fleet, and it is arithmetic, not opinion.

back-of-envelope.text: In a design review someone asks "how many servers?" and the room goes quiet. Estimation is the skill that answers it: from daily active users and a couple of per-user actions you derive requests per second, then storage per year, then bandwidth — the numbers that decide whether one box suffices or you need a sharded fleet. This lesson turns "it depends" into a defended calculation.

Capacity estimation is the sizing step of every design. The chain is mechanical: DAU (daily active users) × actions/user/day = requests/day; divide by 86,400 seconds to get AVERAGE RPS; multiply by a PEAK FACTOR (traffic is not uniform — a common rule of thumb is that the busy period carries several times the average, so designers often use 2–10×) to size for the spike. For storage: records/day × bytes/record × retention → bytes. For bandwidth: RPS × bytes/response. These estimates are order-of-magnitude, not exact, and that is the point — they tell you which architecture class you are in.

back-of-envelope.prompt: Before reading: 100 million DAU each doing 10 writes/day. What is the average writes-per-second, and why is that not the number you provision for?
back-of-envelope.reveal: 100e6 × 10 = 1e9 writes/day. 1e9 / 86,400 ≈ 11,574 average writes/sec. You do NOT provision for the average because traffic is bursty — the daily peak can be several times the mean. Apply a peak factor (say 3–5×) → provision for ~35k–58k writes/sec. Sizing to the average guarantees you fall over at peak.

back-of-envelope.intro: The estimation chain from product numbers to RPS, storage, and bandwidth.
steps: DAU × actions/user/day = total actions/day.
actions/day ÷ 86,400 = average RPS; this is the baseline, not the target.
average RPS × peak factor = peak RPS — always size for the peak.
records/day × bytes/record × 365 × retention = storage; peak RPS × bytes/response = bandwidth.
back-of-envelope.commonMistake: Provisioning for average RPS and forgetting the peak factor. Real traffic has daily and event-driven spikes several times the mean, so an average-sized system is saturated exactly when it matters most.

back-of-envelope.text: Back-of-the-envelope estimation is deliberately crude arithmetic whose job is to place you in the right architecture class — single box, one beefy DB, or a sharded fleet with caches and a CDN. The load chain: DAU × actions/user/day gives actions/day; divide by 86,400 (seconds in a day) for AVERAGE requests/sec. Because real traffic is bursty (a daily peak, a launch spike), you multiply by a PEAK FACTOR — a rule-of-thumb multiplier, commonly in the 2–10× range depending on the product — and provision for that peak RPS, never the mean. The storage chain: records/day × bytes/record × 365 × retention-years gives total bytes; keep a factor for indexes and replication. The bandwidth chain: peak RPS × bytes/response gives peak egress. Two disciplines make these useful: round aggressively (1 day ≈ 86,400 s ≈ 1e5; 1 year ≈ 3e7 s) so you can do it in your head, and treat every output as order-of-magnitude — the goal is to know whether you are at 10 RPS or 100,000 RPS, because that difference, not the third significant figure, is what changes the design.

storyboard.say: Someone asks how many servers you need — the answer starts with two product numbers: daily active users and actions per user per day.
Multiply DAU by actions per user and you have total actions per day — the root number every other estimate derives from.
Divide actions per day by 86,400 seconds and you get average requests per second — the mean load on the system.
But traffic is bursty, so multiply the average by a peak factor of two to ten — you provision for the spike, never the mean.
The same actions-per-day number branches to storage: multiply by bytes per record and retention to get storage per year.
Finally, peak RPS times bytes per response gives peak bandwidth — the pipe you must be able to fill at the worst moment.
The chain is crude on purpose: two product numbers place you in an architecture class — one box, one beefy database, or a sharded fleet.

building-blocks.proof: A request-path classifier that assigns each component its correct role and rejects a path that puts a component in the wrong place.
building-blocks.unlock: You can trace a read and a write request through the standard blocks and say why each hop exists.
building-blocks.outcome: Name the core components of a web system (client, load balancer, app server, cache, database, queue, object store) and trace a request through the path, knowing what each block is for.
building-blocks.doNotClaim: Don't claim to know an architecture because you can list its boxes — you know it when you can trace a request through them and justify each hop.

building-blocks.text: A new engineer sees "client → LB → app → cache → DB → queue" and can name each box but cannot say why a read hits the cache before the DB, or why the queue is off the critical path. The blocks only mean something as a request PATH. This lesson wires the boxes into the journey a request actually takes and the job each block does on the way.

Nearly every web backend is assembled from the same handful of building blocks, each with one job. The CLIENT initiates. The LOAD BALANCER spreads requests across identical app servers and hides failures. The APP SERVER holds business logic and is kept stateless so any instance can serve any request. The CACHE answers hot reads fast to spare the database. The DATABASE is the durable source of truth. The QUEUE decouples slow or bursty work so it happens asynchronously off the request path. The OBJECT STORE holds large blobs (images, files). Knowing the blocks is table stakes; knowing the PATH — and why each hop exists — is the actual skill.

building-blocks.prompt: Before reading: in a read request, why does the app server check the cache before the database? And why is sending a welcome email put on a queue instead of done inline?
building-blocks.reveal: The cache is checked first because it serves hot reads in microseconds and shields the database from the majority of traffic — a cache hit means the DB never sees the request. The welcome email goes on a queue because it is slow and non-critical: doing it inline would block the user's response on an external mail service. The queue lets the request return immediately while a worker sends the email asynchronously — decoupling latency-critical from latency-tolerant work.

building-blocks.intro: The standard read path and where each block sits, plus what belongs off the path.
steps: The load balancer sits in front so any app server can serve any request (they are stateless).
The cache is read before the database; a hit spares the DB entirely.
The database is the durable source of truth, hit on a cache miss.
Slow, non-critical work (email, image processing) goes on a queue, off the request path.
building-blocks.commonMistake: Putting state in the app server (a user session in local memory). It breaks the moment the load balancer sends the next request to a different instance — app servers must be stateless so any of them can handle any request.

building-blocks.text: A web system is a small set of components arranged so a request flows through them, each doing exactly one job. The CLIENT sends the request. The LOAD BALANCER receives it and forwards to one of several identical, STATELESS app servers — statelessness is what lets it route freely and survive an instance dying. The APP SERVER runs business logic and, for a read, consults the CACHE first: a cache hit returns in microseconds and the request never touches the database, which is the whole point — the cache absorbs the hot majority of traffic. On a cache miss it reads the DATABASE, the durable source of truth, and typically populates the cache on the way back. Writes go to the database (and invalidate or update the cache). Work that is slow or non-urgent — sending email, generating thumbnails, updating analytics — is pushed onto a QUEUE and handled by a WORKER asynchronously, so it never adds latency to the user's request. Large binary blobs live in an OBJECT STORE, not the relational database. The skill is not naming these boxes; it is tracing a specific request through them and justifying every hop — why the cache is before the DB, why the app server holds no state, why the queue is off the critical path.
building-blocks.title: The blocks are a request path, and each hop has one job
The standard request path
building-blocks.subtitle: each block one job; slow work is queued off-path

storyboard.say: Every request starts at the client, which sends it to the load balancer — the single front door for the whole system.
The load balancer routes to any app server it likes — the servers are stateless, so every instance is interchangeable and one dying costs nothing.
For a read, the app server asks the cache first: a hit returns in microseconds and the request never touches the database at all.
Only on a cache miss do we fall through to the database — the durable source of truth — and the answer refills the cache on the way back.
Anything slow — emails, thumbnails, reports — is not done here; the app just drops a job on the queue and responds to the user immediately.
A worker consumes that job off the critical path, at its own pace — if it is slow or fails, the user's request never feels it.
That is the whole design: one job per box, cache before database, and slow work queued aside so the request path stays fast and hard to kill.

optionA.text: Enqueue the job and return immediately; a worker processes it async. The user gets a fast response and a spike in uploads becomes a growing queue, not timeouts.

building-blocks.guidance: Queue it (A) when the work is slow and the user does not need the result synchronously — decoupling protects request latency and absorbs bursts. options: Caches guarantee stronger consistency than the database, so reading them first always returns the most up-to-date value.
The cache is the durable source of truth, so reading it first protects the data the database might lose on a crash.
The database cannot serve reads directly; it only accepts writes, so reads must be routed through the cache in front of it.
A cache hit answers in microseconds and means the database never serves that request, absorbing the hot majority of reads.
building-blocks.question: Why is the cache consulted before the database on a read?
building-blocks.explanation: The cache holds hot data and answers in microseconds; a hit means the database never sees that request, so the cache absorbs the majority of read traffic. The database is the durable source of truth, hit only on a miss — the cache is faster and less durable, the opposite of option A.

latency-throughput-availability.unlock: You can explain why tail latency matters, and compute a system's availability from its components' 9s.
latency-throughput-availability.outcome: Reason with the three core system metrics: latency (and why you report p50/p95/p99, not the mean), throughput, and availability — including how availability composes across serial and redundant components.
latency-throughput-availability.doNotClaim: Don't claim a system is "fast" from an average latency — the tail (p99) is what users feel, and availability is a computed product, not a wish.

latency-throughput-availability.text: A dashboard shows 20ms average latency and the team calls the service fast — yet support tickets pile up about slow pages. The average hid a brutal p99 of 2 seconds affecting one request in a hundred, and at scale that is a lot of angry users. Meanwhile leadership wants "four nines" but the design chains five services in series, each at three nines, which cannot possibly reach it. This lesson makes latency percentiles and availability composition into numbers you compute, not adjectives you assert.

Three metrics describe how well a system performs. LATENCY is how long one request takes; because a few slow requests dominate user pain, you report PERCENTILES — p50 (median), p95, p99 — never just the mean, which a handful of huge outliers can distort. THROUGHPUT is how many requests/sec the system sustains. AVAILABILITY is the fraction of time it is up, quoted in "nines": 99.9% (three nines) is ~8.8 hours down/year, 99.99% (four nines) ~52 minutes/year — each extra nine cuts downtime 10×. Crucially, availability COMPOSES: services in SERIES multiply (all must be up, so the system is worse than its weakest link), while REDUNDANT copies in PARALLEL multiply their unavailabilities (only one must be up, so redundancy improves it).

latency-throughput-availability.prompt: Before reading: a request passes through 4 independent services in series, each 99.9% available. Is the end-to-end availability higher or lower than 99.9%, and roughly what is it?
latency-throughput-availability.reveal: Lower. In series, ALL four must be up, so you MULTIPLY: 0.999^4 ≈ 0.996, i.e. about 99.6% — worse than any single component. Chaining dependencies erodes availability; every hop you add in series drags the total down. To get it back up you either remove hops or add redundancy (parallel copies) at the weak points.

latency-throughput-availability.intro: Compose availability across serial dependencies (product) and redundant replicas (parallel).
steps: Latency is reported as percentiles (p50/p95/p99) because the tail is what users feel.
Series availability = product of components; the system is worse than the weakest link.
Parallel (redundant) availability = 1 − (product of unavailabilities); redundancy raises it.
To hit a target, remove serial hops or add parallel redundancy at the weak component.
latency-throughput-availability.commonMistake: Reporting or optimizing the MEAN latency. A mean of 20ms can hide a p99 of 2s; at 1000 req/s that tail is 10 slow requests every second. Users experience the tail, so you must track and target p95/p99.

latency-throughput-availability.text: Three numbers govern performance, and each has a subtlety that separates a real answer from a vibe. LATENCY: the mean lies, because a small number of very slow requests barely move the average but define the user experience — so you report PERCENTILES. p50 is the median, p99 is the value 99% of requests beat; a p99 of 2s means 1 in 100 users waits 2 seconds, and at scale "1 in 100" is thousands of people. THROUGHPUT is requests/sec sustained, and it trades against latency once queues build. AVAILABILITY is uptime fraction in NINES, where each nine is a 10× cut in downtime: 99% ≈ 3.65 days/year down, 99.9% ≈ 8.8 hours, 99.99% ≈ 52 minutes, 99.999% ≈ 5 minutes. The load-bearing insight is COMPOSITION. When a request depends on several components IN SERIES (all must succeed), their availabilities MULTIPLY — 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.997 — so the whole is always LESS available than its weakest part, and adding dependencies makes it worse. When you add REDUNDANT replicas IN PARALLEL (only one need succeed), you multiply their UNAVAILABILITIES: two 99% replicas give 1 − 0.01×0.01 = 99.99%. That is why hitting a high availability target is not aspiration but arithmetic: count your serial hops, find the weakest, and add parallelism until the product clears the goal.
latency-throughput-availability.title: Tail latency is felt; availability is multiplied
Availability composition
latency-throughput-availability.subtitle: series multiplies down; redundancy multiplies unavailability

storyboard.say: Every request starts at the client and must pass through service A, which is up 99.9 percent of the time — about 8.8 hours of downtime a year.
Service A sits in series with what comes next, and series components multiply availabilities — every dependency you chain drags the total down.
Service B runs as two replicas at 99 percent each; the path fails only if both die at once, so you multiply unavailabilities: 1 percent times 1 percent.
That 0.01 percent joint failure turns two mediocre boxes into 99.99 percent — redundancy buys nearly two extra nines from ordinary hardware.
Now compose the whole path: 99.9 percent times 99.99 percent is about 99.89 — the series chain, not the redundant pair, sets your ceiling.
So four nines is a design property, not a wish: series multiplies you down, parallel multiplies failure away — count the nines along the entire path.

latency-throughput-availability.symptom: A design promises 99.99% availability, but it is a linear chain of five microservices each rated 99.9%, and it keeps missing the SLO.

optionA.text: Run two instances in parallel; only one needs to be up. Two 99.9% replicas give ~99.9999% — redundancy multiplies unavailability down cheaply and survives a single instance failure.
optionA.label: Add a redundant replica

optionB.text: Invest in better hardware, retries, and code to lift one box. Real gains are marginal and it still has a single point of failure — one crash is 100% down.
optionB.label: Harden the single instance

latency-throughput-availability.guidance: Add redundancy (A) for availability — parallelism attacks the math directly and removes the single point of failure, which hardening never can. Use B for latency or correctness fixes, but availability targets are met by removing serial single points and adding parallel copies.
latency-throughput-availability.question: You must raise a component from 99.9% to 99.99%. Add a redundant replica, or make the single instance more reliable?

options: 98% — multiply the two availabilities (0.99 × 0.99), since both copies have to be working for the pair to work.
100% — with a redundant backup there is always one node up, so the pair simply never has any downtime at all.
99% — a second copy is only a spare, so the redundant pair is no more available than a single one of the nodes.
99.99% — multiply the unavailabilities (0.01 × 0.01); the redundant pair fails only when both nodes fail at once.
latency-throughput-availability.question: Two components each 99% available. What is their availability if they are REDUNDANT (parallel, only one need be up)?
latency-throughput-availability.explanation: For redundant components you multiply the UNAVAILABILITIES: both must fail for the pair to fail, so P(both down) = 0.01 × 0.01 = 0.0001, giving availability 1 − 0.0001 = 99.99%. Multiplying the availabilities (0.99 × 0.99 = 98%) is the SERIES formula, which applies when both must be up, not when either suffices.

sql-vs-nosql.proof: A store-selector that recommends a store class from the workload's access pattern and consistency needs, and refuses a mismatch.
sql-vs-nosql.unlock: You can justify a store choice by the queries and consistency the workload actually needs.
sql-vs-nosql.outcome: Choose a data store from the ACCESS PATTERN, not fashion: relational for rich queries/transactions/joins, key-value for point lookups, document for nested aggregates, wide-column for huge write throughput.
sql-vs-nosql.doNotClaim: Don't claim "NoSQL is faster" or "SQL doesn't scale" — the right store is the one whose model matches your access pattern.

sql-vs-nosql.text: A team picks a document database because it is trendy, then discovers their core feature needs multi-row transactions and ad-hoc joins the store cannot do — so they bolt joins into application code and lose consistency. The store should have been chosen from the ACCESS PATTERN. This lesson turns "SQL or NoSQL?" into a decision driven by the queries and guarantees the workload demands.

Data stores differ by the DATA MODEL and the guarantees they optimize for. RELATIONAL (SQL: Postgres, MySQL) gives normalized tables, JOINs, secondary indexes, and ACID transactions — ideal when data is highly related and you need strong consistency and flexible queries. KEY-VALUE (Redis, DynamoDB) is a giant hash map: blazing point reads/writes by key, but no rich query. DOCUMENT (MongoDB) stores nested JSON aggregates — good when you read/write a whole object at once and rarely join. WIDE-COLUMN (Cassandra) is built for massive write throughput and horizontal scale with tunable consistency, at the cost of ad-hoc query flexibility. The choice follows the access pattern: what do you query BY, do you need joins/transactions, and how strong must consistency be.

sql-vs-nosql.prompt: Before reading: your workload is "look up a user session by session-id, millions of times per second, no joins, no reporting." Which store class fits, and why not relational?
sql-vs-nosql.reveal: A KEY-VALUE store fits: the entire access pattern is point lookup by a single key at very high rate, which a hash-map-shaped store serves in O(1) with trivial horizontal scaling. Relational is over-powered here — its joins, secondary indexes, and ACID overhead buy you nothing for a pure key lookup and add latency and operational weight. Match the store to the pattern; do not pay for query power you never use.

sql-vs-nosql.intro: Pick a store class from the access pattern and consistency requirement.
steps: If the workload needs multi-row transactions or joins → relational.
If it is pure point lookup by key at high rate → key-value.
If you read/write whole nested objects and rarely join → document.
If write throughput is massive and consistency can be tuned → wide-column.
sql-vs-nosql.commonMistake: Choosing a store by popularity ("everyone uses Mongo") instead of the access pattern, then reimplementing joins or transactions in application code — which is slower, buggier, and loses the consistency the database would have given you for free.

sql-vs-nosql.text: There is no universally "faster" or "more scalable" database — there are data models optimized for different ACCESS PATTERNS, and the engineering skill is matching them. RELATIONAL stores (Postgres, MySQL) normalize data into tables and give you JOINs, secondary indexes, and ACID transactions; choose them when your data is richly interconnected and you need strong consistency or ad-hoc queries — which is most transactional applications. KEY-VALUE stores are hash maps at scale: O(1) get/put by key, effortless horizontal partitioning, but no query beyond the key — choose them for sessions, caches, and lookups where the key is always known. DOCUMENT stores keep denormalized nested aggregates (a whole order with its line-items as one JSON doc); choose them when you fetch and mutate a complete object at once and joins are rare. WIDE-COLUMN stores (Cassandra) are engineered for enormous write throughput and linear horizontal scale with TUNABLE consistency, trading away ad-hoc query flexibility. The decision procedure is always the same three questions: what do I query BY, do I need joins or multi-row transactions, and how strong must consistency be. Answer those from the workload and the store falls out — and the classic failure is inverting it: picking the store first and then contorting the workload (hand-rolled joins, application-level transactions) to fit a model that never suited it.
sql-vs-nosql.title: The access pattern picks the store, not the trend
Store selection by access pattern
sql-vs-nosql.subtitle: the workload questions route to a store class

storyboard.say: Never pick a database by trend — start from the workload's access pattern, because every store class optimizes a different data model.
First question: does the workload need joins or multi-row transactions? That single answer decides most transactional apps.
If yes, choose relational SQL — Postgres or MySQL give you joins, secondary indexes, and ACID; bolting joins into app code loses consistency.
If not, ask whether every read is a point lookup by a known key — sessions, caches, simple lookups fit this shape.
When the key is always known, key-value stores like Redis or DynamoDB give O(1) gets and easy partitioning — but no query beyond the key.
Otherwise ask if the data is a nested aggregate read as one unit — if yes, a document store fits; if writes are huge and columnar, go wide-column.
The insight: there is no universally faster database — the skill is matching the store's data model to your access pattern, in this exact order.

A relational DB does key lookups fine and gives you reports for free; only split to a KV hot path (B) when measured scale forces it — premature splitting adds two systems to keep in sync.
sql-vs-nosql.question: Your app is mostly point lookups by key, but has a few reporting queries. One relational store, or a key-value store plus something for reports?

options: Key-value — a hash-map-shaped store matches point lookups by key exactly and partitions horizontally with ease.
Any store works; for a plain key lookup the data model is irrelevant, so just pick whichever the team already runs.
Document — nesting related fields into one aggregate is what makes single-key reads fast, so a document store fits.
Relational — its ACID transactions and join engine are what keep high-rate key lookups fast and correct at scale.
sql-vs-nosql.question: A workload is pure O(1) point lookup by a known key, at very high rate, with no joins or ad-hoc queries. Which store class fits best?
sql-vs-nosql.explanation: The access pattern is entirely get-by-key at high rate — exactly what a key-value (hash-map-shaped) store optimizes, with trivial partitioning. Relational query power and ACID overhead buy nothing here; the model does matter, because the store is optimized around the access pattern.

indexing.proof: A query-cost estimator that compares scan cost vs index cost using selectivity and recommends whether the index helps.
indexing.unlock: You can predict when an index speeds a query up, when it is ignored, and what it costs on writes.
indexing.outcome: Understand how a B-tree index turns an O(n) scan into an O(log n) lookup, why selectivity decides whether the index is even used, and the write/storage cost every index adds.
indexing.doNotClaim: Don't claim "add an index" fixes every slow query — a low-selectivity index is ignored, and every index taxes writes.

indexing.text: A query over 10 million rows takes 4 seconds; someone adds an index and it is instant — then someone adds an index to every column and writes slow to a crawl while some queries still scan. Indexes are a precise tool: they help HIGH-SELECTIVITY lookups by turning a full scan into a tree descent, they are ignored for low-selectivity predicates, and they cost you on every write. This lesson makes the index decision a computed one.

A database index is an auxiliary structure — usually a B-tree — that lets the engine find matching rows without scanning the table. A full table scan is O(n): read every row. A B-tree index makes an equality or range lookup O(log n): descend the tree to the leaf, then walk the range. But the optimizer only USES an index when the predicate is SELECTIVE enough — if a query matches most rows, jumping around the index plus fetching each row costs more than a straight sequential scan, so the planner picks the scan. And every index must be updated on every insert/update/delete and consumes storage, so indexes speed reads at the cost of writes. The craft is indexing the columns your selective queries filter/sort by — and no more.

indexing.prompt: Before reading: you index a "country" column, but 90% of rows are country = "US". Will a query for country = "US" use the index? What about country = "IS" (0.1% of rows)?
indexing.reveal: The "US" query (90% selectivity — matches most rows) will likely NOT use the index: fetching 90% of the table via random index lookups is slower than one sequential scan, so the planner scans. The "IS" query (0.1% — highly selective) WILL use the index: it isolates a tiny fraction of rows, turning an O(n) scan into an O(log n) descent plus a few fetches. Selectivity — the fraction of rows a predicate matches — decides whether an index is worth using.

indexing.intro: Estimate scan cost vs index cost from row count and selectivity, and decide.
steps: Scan cost grows with total rows (O(n)); index lookup cost is log(rows) plus one fetch per matched row.
Selectivity = fraction of rows matched; low selectivity (few matches) favors the index.
High selectivity (many matches) makes per-row index fetches cost more than a scan.
Every index also adds write cost and storage — count that against the read speedup.
indexing.commonMistake: Indexing every column "to be safe." Each index slows every write and consumes storage, and low-selectivity indexes are never even used — so you pay the write tax for zero read benefit. Index the columns your selective queries actually filter or sort by.

indexing.text: An index is a sorted auxiliary structure, classically a B-TREE, that the database maintains alongside a table so it can locate rows without reading all of them. Without an index, finding matching rows is a full table SCAN: O(n), every row read. With a B-tree index, an equality or range predicate becomes an O(log n) descent to the leaf followed by a walk across the matching range — the difference between 10,000,000 reads and ~24 tree steps. But two facts keep this from being free. First, SELECTIVITY governs whether the index is used at all: selectivity is the fraction of rows a predicate matches, and the optimizer compares the index plan (log n descent + one random fetch per matched row) against a sequential scan (n cheap sequential reads). When a predicate matches a large fraction of the table, the many random fetches lose to a single scan, so the planner IGNORES the index — an index on a column where 90% of rows share one value does nothing for the common query. Highly selective predicates (matching a tiny fraction) are exactly where an index wins. Second, an index is not read-only: every insert, update, and delete must also update every affected index, and each index consumes storage, so indexes accelerate reads at a direct WRITE cost. The discipline: index the columns your selective queries filter and sort by, verify the planner actually uses them, and delete indexes that earn nothing.
indexing.title: An index trades write cost for O(log n) reads — only when selective
Scan vs index by selectivity
indexing.subtitle: the planner picks the cheaper path

storyboard.say: A query arrives with a predicate over ten million rows, and the planner's first job is deciding how to find the matches.
The key question is selectivity: what fraction of the table does this predicate actually match?
If the predicate matches many rows, the planner chooses a sequential scan and simply reads every row in order.
If it matches only a few rows, the B-tree wins: an O of log n descent to the leaf, then fetch just the matches.
But the index is never free: every insert and update must maintain the tree, so each index adds a write and storage tax.
So indexes are a precise tool: add them for selective lookups the planner will actually use, and skip them everywhere else.

indexing.guidance: Add the index (A) when the query is frequent AND selective — that is precisely where a B-tree pays off and the write cost of one index is small. Indexes only serve ORDER BY, never WHERE, so a filtering query cannot use one no matter how selective it happens to be.
Indexes only accelerate numeric columns, so the planner ignores an index built on text or other non-numeric types.
The predicate has low selectivity — it matches most rows, so one sequential scan beats many random index fetches.
indexing.question: Why might the query planner refuse to use an index on a column even though one exists?
indexing.explanation: When a predicate matches a large fraction of rows (low selectivity), fetching each match through the index costs more than one straight sequential scan, so the cost-based planner chooses the scan. Indexes win on HIGH-selectivity predicates that isolate a small fraction of rows.

replication.proof: A replication-lag checker that decides whether a given read can be served from a follower without violating read-after-write consistency.
replication.unlock: You can explain replication lag and route reads to avoid the read-your-own-writes anomaly.
replication.outcome: Understand leader/follower replication, the sync-vs-async durability/latency tradeoff, and the read-after-write anomaly that async replication lag creates.
replication.doNotClaim: Don't claim followers are "just extra copies" — async replication lags, and a naive read from a follower can miss the user's own just-made write.

replication.text: A user updates their profile, the app reads it back from a follower replica, and the OLD value comes back — because the write went to the leader and the follower has not caught up yet. Replication is how you scale reads and survive a node loss, but async replicas LAG, and that lag produces real anomalies. This lesson makes the lag visible and teaches you to route reads so a user always sees their own writes.

Replication keeps copies of the data on multiple nodes for read scaling and fault tolerance. The common model is LEADER/FOLLOWER: all writes go to the LEADER, which streams a change log to one or more FOLLOWERS that serve reads. The key choice is SYNCHRONOUS vs ASYNCHRONOUS. Sync replication waits for a follower to acknowledge before the write is confirmed — durable and consistent, but slower and stalls if a follower is down. Async confirms the write as soon as the leader has it and ships to followers in the background — fast and available, but followers LAG, so a read from a follower may return stale data. That lag causes the READ-AFTER-WRITE (read-your-own-writes) anomaly: a user who just wrote can read their own stale value from a lagging follower. The fix is to route a user's reads to the leader (or a caught-up follower) for a window after their write.

replication.prompt: Before reading: with async leader/follower replication, a user updates their name and the app immediately reads it from a follower. What can go wrong, and how do you prevent it?
replication.reveal: The follower may not have received the update yet (replication lag), so the read returns the OLD name — the user does not see their own write, which looks like a bug. Prevention: for a short window after a user's write, route THAT user's reads to the leader or to a follower known to be caught up past the write's position. This "read-your-writes" routing trades a little leader load for correctness the user can feel.

replication.intro: Decide if a follower read is safe given its replication position vs the write position.
steps: Writes go to the leader and get a monotonically increasing log position.
Followers apply the leader's log and report the position they have reached.
A follower read is safe only if the follower's position ≥ the user's last-write position.
If the follower is behind the user's write, route that read to the leader.
replication.commonMistake: Load-balancing all reads across followers without tracking each user's last write. Right after a write, the user's read lands on a lagging follower and returns stale data — the read-your-own-writes anomaly, which looks like data loss to the user.

replication.text: Replication puts copies of the data on multiple nodes to scale reads and survive failures, and the workhorse model is LEADER/FOLLOWER (a.k.a. primary/replica): every write is applied at the LEADER, which appends it to a replication log at a monotonically increasing position and streams that log to FOLLOWERS, which apply it and serve reads. The pivotal choice is durability vs latency. SYNCHRONOUS replication holds the write "unconfirmed" until at least one follower acknowledges it — the data survives a leader crash and reads are consistent, but every write pays a round-trip and stalls entirely if the sync follower is unavailable. ASYNCHRONOUS replication confirms the write as soon as the leader has durably stored it and ships to followers in the background — writes are fast and stay available even if a follower is down, but followers LAG behind the leader by some replication delay. That lag is not academic: it produces the READ-AFTER-WRITE anomaly, where a user who just updated a value reads it back from a follower that has not yet applied the update and sees the OLD value — indistinguishable from a bug or data loss to that user. The standard fix is position-aware routing: record the log position of a user's latest write, and serve their subsequent reads only from a replica whose applied position has caught up to (≥) that write — otherwise send the read to the leader. This buys read-your-own-writes consistency for the cost of a little extra leader traffic in the window right after each write.

storyboard.say: A user updates their profile: the write goes to the leader, which commits it at log position N and confirms immediately.
The leader streams its replication log to the followers, which apply each change in order and serve the read traffic.
Because replication is asynchronous, one follower is already caught up to N, but the other is still behind — it holds the old profile.
Moments later the same user reads their profile back; hit the lagging follower and they see stale data — their own write vanishes.
The fix is read-your-writes routing: the router remembers the user wrote at position N and only picks a follower that has replayed to N or beyond.
If no follower has reached N yet, the router falls back to the leader — lag never disappears, so you route reads around it, not hope it's zero.

sharding-partitioning.proof: A consistent-hash ring that distributes keys across nodes and reports the per-node key counts so you can see balance and hotspots.
sharding-partitioning.unlock: You can choose a shard key that avoids hotspots and explain why consistent hashing minimizes reshuffling when a node joins or leaves.
sharding-partitioning.outcome: Split data across nodes by a shard key, understand why the key choice determines load balance, and use consistent hashing to spread keys evenly and detect hotspots.
sharding-partitioning.doNotClaim: Don't claim sharding "just splits the data" — a bad shard key creates a hotspot that overloads one node while the others idle.

sharding-partitioning.text: A service shards user data by "signup month" and one node melts under all the new users while older-month nodes sit idle — a classic HOTSPOT from a bad shard key. Sharding scales writes and storage past a single node, but only if the KEY spreads load evenly, and only if adding a node does not reshuffle everything. This lesson builds the consistent-hash ring that makes both true, and a hotspot detector to prove the spread.

Sharding (horizontal partitioning) splits a dataset across multiple nodes so writes, storage, and throughput scale beyond one machine — each node owns a subset of the keys. The SHARD KEY decides which node a record lands on, and choosing it well is the whole game: a key with skewed distribution (few hot values) piles load on one node (a HOTSPOT) while others idle. Naive modulo sharding (node = hash(key) % N) spreads keys, but changing N remaps almost every key. CONSISTENT HASHING (Karger et al., 1997) fixes that: hash both keys and nodes onto a ring; each key is owned by the next node clockwise, so adding or removing a node only remaps the keys between it and its neighbor — about K/N keys on average, the theoretical minimum. Virtual nodes (many ring positions per physical node) smooth the distribution further.

sharding-partitioning.prompt: Before reading: you shard 8 keys across 4 nodes with node = hash(key) % 4. You add a 5th node (% 5). Roughly how many of the 8 keys move? Why does consistent hashing do better?
sharding-partitioning.reveal: With modulo, changing 4→5 changes hash % N for almost every key, so most of the 8 keys move — a near-total reshuffle that invalidates caches and thrashes the network. Consistent hashing places nodes on a hash ring and gives each key to the next node clockwise; adding a node only steals the keys in the arc between it and its clockwise neighbor — on average about K/N keys (here ~1–2 of 8), not most of them. That minimal-movement property is why consistent hashing underpins distributed caches and databases.

sharding-partitioning.intro: Build a consistent-hash ring: place nodes on the ring, then assign each key to the next node clockwise.
steps: Hash each NODE to a position on a fixed ring.
Hash each KEY to a ring position; its owner is the first node clockwise (≥ its position).
Wrap around: a key past the last node belongs to the first node.
Count keys per node to see the distribution and spot hotspots.
sharding-partitioning.commonMistake: Choosing a low-cardinality or skewed shard key (country, signup-month, a boolean). Most records collapse onto a few values, so a few nodes carry nearly all the load — a hotspot — while the rest idle. A good shard key has high cardinality and even distribution.

sharding-partitioning.text: Sharding scales a store horizontally by splitting the keyspace across nodes, and two problems decide whether it works: load BALANCE and reshuffling COST. Balance depends entirely on the SHARD KEY. If the key is skewed or low-cardinality — country, signup month, a status flag — records pile onto a handful of values and the nodes owning them become HOTSPOTS, saturated while their peers sit idle; a good shard key is high-cardinality and uniformly distributed (a user id, a hashed key). Reshuffling cost is the other trap: with naive modulo sharding, node = hash(key) % N, changing the node count N alters hash % N for nearly every key, so scaling out remaps almost the entire dataset and invalidates every cache. CONSISTENT HASHING (Karger, Lehman, Leighton, Panigrahy, Levine, Lewin, 1997) solves this by mapping both keys and nodes onto the same circular hash space; each key is owned by the first node encountered going CLOCKWISE from the key's position (wrapping past the end back to the first node). Now adding or removing a node only affects the keys in the arc between that node and its neighbor — on average about K/N of K total keys, which is the minimum any scheme can achieve. Because a single hash position per node can still leave uneven gaps, real systems assign each physical node many VIRTUAL positions on the ring, which averages out the arc sizes and smooths the distribution. This is the mechanism under Dynamo, Cassandra, and consistent-hash load balancers alike: even spread, minimal movement on membership change.

storyboard.say: Every record starts with its shard key — we hash that key onto a fixed ring of positions, so placement depends on the key, not on the node count.
From the key's hash position, we walk clockwise around the ring; the first node we hit — here node A — owns that key.
Nodes B and C own the next arcs, so the keyspace is carved into ranges — each node serves only the slice of hashes that lands on its arc.
Now the payoff: adding a node just splits one arc, so only about K over N keys move — modulo sharding would remap nearly the whole dataset.
But the ring can't save a bad key: shard by signup month and every new user hashes to the same few values, melting one node while its peers idle.
So sharding works when two things hold — a high-cardinality, uniform shard key for balance, and consistent hashing to keep rescaling cheap.

Inserting a node only reassigns the keys in the arc between it and its clockwise neighbor — roughly K/N of K keys — instead of re-evaluating hash % N for every key, which modulo sharding does. That minimal movement (proven optimal) is the defining property of consistent hashing.

caching-strategies.proof: A working LRU cache that evicts the least-recently-used entry at capacity and reports the hit rate over a request trace.
caching-strategies.unlock: You can pick a caching strategy for a workload and predict its hit rate and staleness behavior.
caching-strategies.outcome: Choose a caching strategy (cache-aside, write-through, write-back) and reason about hit rate, TTL, and eviction — implementing an LRU cache and measuring its hit rate.
caching-strategies.doNotClaim: Don't claim a cache "makes things fast" without a hit rate — a cache with a low hit rate adds a hop and buys nothing.

caching-strategies.text: A team adds a cache and latency barely improves, because the hit rate is 20% — most requests miss, pay the cache lookup AND the database read. Caching is not a magic speed switch; it is a strategy with a measurable hit rate, an eviction policy that decides what survives, and a TTL that bounds staleness. This lesson builds a real LRU cache and measures the number that actually matters: the hit rate.

A cache stores hot data on a fast tier so repeated reads skip the slow store. Three write strategies decide correctness and speed. CACHE-ASIDE (lazy): the app checks the cache; on a miss it reads the DB and populates the cache — simple, and only requested data is cached. WRITE-THROUGH: writes go to the cache AND the DB synchronously — the cache is always fresh, at higher write latency. WRITE-BACK (write-behind): writes hit the cache and flush to the DB later — fastest writes, but a crash can lose un-flushed data. Because a cache is finite, it needs an EVICTION policy; LRU (least-recently-used) evicts the entry unused for the longest, a good fit when recent data is likely to be reused. TTL caps how long an entry lives regardless of use, bounding staleness. The metric that decides if any of it helped is the HIT RATE: hits / (hits + misses).

caching-strategies.prompt: Before reading: an LRU cache holds 2 entries. Requests come in: A, B, A, C. Which key gets evicted when C arrives, and why?
caching-strategies.reveal: B is evicted. After A, B the cache holds {A, B}. The request for A makes A the most-recently-used, so the order (LRU→MRU) is B, A. When C arrives the cache is full, so it evicts the LEAST-recently-used entry — B — leaving {A, C}. LRU keeps what was touched most recently on the bet that recent access predicts near-future access.

caching-strategies.intro: An LRU cache: a Map ordered by recency, evicting the oldest entry at capacity.
steps: A Map keeps entries in insertion order; the first key is the least-recently-used.
On get, delete+reinsert the key so it becomes most-recently-used; count hit or miss.
On put at capacity, evict the first (oldest) key before inserting.
Hit rate = hits / (hits + misses) — the number that says whether the cache earns its place.
caching-strategies.commonMistake: Deploying a cache and never measuring the hit rate. A cache with a poor hit rate adds a network hop and memory cost while most requests still hit the database — you must measure hits/(hits+misses) to know the cache is actually working.

caching-strategies.text: A cache trades memory for latency by keeping hot data on a fast tier, but "add a cache" is three real decisions. The WRITE STRATEGY governs freshness and speed: CACHE-ASIDE (the app reads through — miss → load from DB → populate) is the default, caching only what is actually requested and tolerating a brief staleness window; WRITE-THROUGH writes to cache and DB together so the cache is never stale, paying extra write latency; WRITE-BACK writes to the cache and flushes to the DB asynchronously for the fastest writes, risking loss of un-flushed data on a crash. Because cache memory is finite, an EVICTION policy decides what to keep when full. LRU — least-recently-used — evicts the entry untouched for the longest, which works because access patterns are usually temporally local: what you read recently you tend to read again. A TTL adds a time bound so an entry expires regardless of use, capping how stale a served value can be. Above all, a cache is judged by its HIT RATE = hits / (hits + misses): a high hit rate means most reads skip the database and latency drops; a low hit rate means you added a hop and some memory for almost nothing. The engineering loop is: pick the write strategy for your freshness needs, pick an eviction policy for your access pattern, set a TTL for your staleness tolerance, then MEASURE the hit rate and tune until the cache earns its cost.

If the key is present, that's a hit: the cache returns immediately from memory and the slow database is skipped entirely.
On a miss you pay twice: the cache lookup was wasted, and now the app must load the value from the database anyway.
The loaded value populates the cache, but memory is finite — if the cache is full, LRU evicts the entry untouched the longest to make room.
The cache reports hits and misses as a metric — hit rate is the number that tells you whether the cache is actually earning its keep.
At a 20 percent hit rate, most reads pay cache plus database — a cache only speeds you up when hot data stays resident and the hit rate is high.

caching-strategies.guidance: Use write-through (A) when writes must be durable and consistent — you accept the latency for safety. Use write-back (B) only for loss-tolerant, write-heavy data (counters, metrics) where throughput matters more than never losing the last few writes. Match the strategy to whether a crash can lose data you care about.

cache-invalidation.proof: A single-flight guard that, when a hot key expires, lets exactly one request recompute while the rest wait for and share that one result.
cache-invalidation.unlock: You can prevent a thundering herd from hammering the origin when a popular cached key expires.
cache-invalidation.outcome: Handle the hard part of caching: staleness after a write, and the cache stampede (thundering herd) when a hot key expires — using a single-flight guard so only one request recomputes.
cache-invalidation.doNotClaim: Don't claim a TTL is enough — when a hot key expires, hundreds of concurrent misses can stampede the database unless one request fills the cache for all.

cache-invalidation.text: A wildly popular item is cached with a 60-second TTL. At the tick it expires, and in that instant 500 concurrent requests all MISS, all hit the database at once, and the origin buckles — a cache STAMPEDE (thundering herd). The cache did its job 99.9% of the time and then caused an outage on expiry. This lesson builds the single-flight guard that lets exactly one request refill the cache while the rest wait for its result.

Two problems make invalidation "one of the two hard things in computer science." STALENESS: after a write, the cached copy is out of date until it is invalidated or its TTL lapses — you must decide how fresh reads must be and invalidate or update the cache on writes accordingly. The STAMPEDE (thundering herd / dogpile): when a HOT key expires, every concurrent request misses simultaneously and all recompute against the origin at once, converting one expiry into a flood. The classic fix is SINGLE-FLIGHT (request coalescing): the first request to miss acquires a lock and recomputes; concurrent requests for the same key do NOT also recompute — they wait on that in-flight computation and share its result. Complementary tactics include serving the stale value while one request refreshes in the background, and jittering TTLs so many keys do not expire at the same instant.

cache-invalidation.prompt: Before reading: a hot key with 500 concurrent readers expires. Without any guard, how many database recomputations happen? With single-flight, how many?
cache-invalidation.reveal: Without a guard: all 500 requests miss at once and all 500 recompute against the database — a stampede that can take the origin down. With single-flight: exactly ONE request recomputes; the other 499 detect an in-flight computation for that key, wait for it, and receive the same freshly-cached result. One recomputation instead of 500 — the origin sees a single load regardless of how many readers arrive at the expiry instant.

cache-invalidation.intro: A single-flight guard: the first miss computes; concurrent misses await the same in-flight promise.
steps: On a miss, check whether a computation for this key is already in flight.
If yes, return that same promise — do NOT start another computation.
If no, start the computation, record it as in-flight, and let others join it.
When it resolves, remove the in-flight entry; all joiners share the one result.
cache-invalidation.commonMistake: Relying on TTL alone for a hot key. The instant it expires, every concurrent reader misses and stampedes the origin — a self-inflicted outage. You need request coalescing (single-flight), stale-while-revalidate, or TTL jitter so one expiry does not become hundreds of simultaneous recomputations.

cache-invalidation.text: Cache invalidation is hard because a cache is a second copy of the truth, and copies drift. The first problem is STALENESS: after the underlying data changes, the cached value is wrong until you invalidate it (delete/refresh on write) or its TTL expires — so you must decide, per data, how stale a read may be and wire invalidation into the write path accordingly. The second, sharper problem is the CACHE STAMPEDE, also called the thundering herd or dogpile: for a HOT key with many concurrent readers, the moment the entry expires ALL of those readers miss at the same instant and ALL recompute against the origin simultaneously, so a routine expiry becomes a synchronized flood that can overwhelm the database — the cache protected you 99.9% of the time and then caused the outage. The primary defense is SINGLE-FLIGHT (a.k.a. request coalescing): when a key is missing, the first request to arrive starts the recomputation and registers it as "in flight"; every other concurrent request for the same key detects that in-flight work and WAITS on it instead of launching its own, so the origin sees exactly one load no matter how many readers pile up. Two complements harden this further: STALE-WHILE-REVALIDATE serves the last known (slightly stale) value immediately while a single background request refreshes it, so no reader blocks; and TTL JITTER spreads expiries randomly so a batch of keys populated together does not all expire on the same tick. Together they ensure that a popular key's expiry costs one recomputation, not a herd.

storyboard.say: A hot key just expired, so 500 concurrent readers all miss the cache in the same instant — this is the makings of a stampede.
Without protection, every one of those misses would hit the database at once; instead, they all funnel into a single-flight guard.
The guard makes the key decision: only the first request through becomes the leader and is allowed to recompute the value.
Everyone else is parked — the other 499 requests simply wait on the leader instead of stampeding the origin themselves.
The leader queries the database exactly once, so the origin sees a single recompute instead of a synchronized flood of 500.
With the fresh value in hand, the leader refills the cache, and every waiter is handed that same shared result.
That's the core insight: collapse N identical misses into one recompute — the herd waits briefly, the origin does the work once.

optionA.text: Return the last known value immediately and refresh in the background with a single request. No reader blocks; the tradeoff is serving briefly stale data during the refresh window.
optionA.label: Stale-while-revalidate

optionB.text: Make readers wait for the recomputation (coalesced via single-flight). Everyone gets fresh data, but they all pause for the recompute latency at the expiry moment.

cache-invalidation.guidance: Prefer stale-while-revalidate (A) when a few seconds of staleness is acceptable — it keeps latency flat through expiries and, combined with single-flight, still hits the origin only once. Block-until-fresh (B) is right only when the data must never be served stale (prices at checkout, permissions). Choose by how much staleness the read can tolerate.

load-balancing.proof: A load balancer that implements round-robin and least-connections and reports the resulting request distribution across healthy backends.
load-balancing.unlock: You can pick a balancing algorithm for a workload and explain how health checks keep traffic off dead backends.
load-balancing.outcome: Distribute requests across backends: understand L4 vs L7, the round-robin / least-connections / consistent-hash algorithms, and health checks that route around failed backends.
load-balancing.doNotClaim: Don't claim a load balancer just "spreads traffic" — the algorithm and health checks decide whether load is even and whether a dead backend still gets requests.

load-balancing.text: A backend crashes and the load balancer keeps sending it one request in three, so a third of users get errors — because there were no health checks. Meanwhile a naive round-robin sends equal requests to backends with wildly different load, and the slow ones pile up. A load balancer is only as good as its ALGORITHM and its HEALTH CHECKS. This lesson implements the algorithms and proves the distribution they produce.

A load balancer (LB) sits in front of a pool of identical backends and distributes requests so no single one is overwhelmed, while hiding failures. It operates at LAYER 4 (transport: routes by IP/port, fast, protocol-agnostic) or LAYER 7 (application: reads HTTP, can route by path/header/cookie, richer but heavier). The ALGORITHM decides who gets each request: ROUND-ROBIN cycles evenly through backends (simple, ignores actual load); LEAST-CONNECTIONS sends the next request to the backend with the fewest in-flight requests (adapts to uneven request durations); CONSISTENT-HASH routes by a key so the same client/session sticks to the same backend (useful for cache locality). HEALTH CHECKS are non-negotiable: the LB periodically probes each backend and removes unhealthy ones from rotation, so a crashed backend stops receiving traffic instead of erroring one request in N.

load-balancing.prompt: Before reading: with round-robin over 3 backends, one backend handles requests that take 10× longer than the others. What goes wrong, and which algorithm fixes it?
load-balancing.reveal: Round-robin gives each backend an equal SHARE of requests regardless of how long each takes, so the backend stuck with slow requests accumulates a growing backlog while the fast ones idle between turns — uneven actual load despite even request counts. LEAST-CONNECTIONS fixes it: it routes each new request to the backend with the fewest in-flight requests, so the slow backend (holding many open connections) stops receiving new work until it drains. It balances load, not just request count.

load-balancing.intro: Round-robin (cycle a pointer) and least-connections (pick the min in-flight) over healthy backends.
steps: Round-robin advances a pointer over the healthy pool, giving each an equal turn.
Least-connections scans the healthy pool and picks the backend with the fewest in-flight requests.
Both operate only over HEALTHY backends — unhealthy ones are excluded from selection.
Health checks flip a backend's healthy flag so failures leave rotation automatically.
load-balancing.commonMistake: Running a load balancer with no health checks. When a backend crashes, round-robin keeps handing it its share of requests, so 1/N of all traffic errors until a human intervenes. The LB must probe backends and pull unhealthy ones from rotation automatically.

load-balancing.text: A load balancer fronts a pool of interchangeable backends and has two jobs: spread work evenly and hide failures. It works at one of two layers. LAYER 4 balances at the transport level (IP/port), forwarding packets without understanding the payload — fast and protocol-agnostic. LAYER 7 balances at the application level, parsing HTTP so it can route by path, header, or cookie and terminate TLS — more capable, more expensive per request. The ALGORITHM chooses the target. ROUND-ROBIN cycles through backends in order, giving each an equal COUNT of requests; it is simple but blind to how much work each request is, so it imbalances when request durations vary. LEAST-CONNECTIONS routes each request to the backend currently handling the fewest in-flight requests, which tracks actual LOAD and self-corrects when some requests run long. CONSISTENT-HASH routes by a request key (client IP, session id) so a given client always lands on the same backend — valuable for session or cache locality — and, being consistent hashing, it barely reshuffles when the backend set changes. Underpinning all of them are HEALTH CHECKS: the LB continuously probes each backend (a TCP connect or an HTTP endpoint) and, on failure, marks it unhealthy and removes it from the selectable pool, so a crashed backend stops receiving traffic instead of erroring one request in N. Without health checks, no algorithm can save you — the LB will faithfully route to a dead node. With them, the pool self-heals: failures leave rotation, recoveries rejoin.

storyboard.say: Every request starts at the client and hits one address: the load balancer, which fronts a pool of identical backends.
The load balancer's first job is spreading work: an algorithm like round-robin or least-connections picks which backend gets each request.
Round-robin gives each backend an equal count of requests, but it is blind to load, so a slow backend quietly piles up work.
Now backend three crashes; without a check, the balancer would keep sending it one request in three and a third of users would see errors.
That is the second job, hiding failures: health checks probe every backend, and backend three stops answering.
After repeated failed probes, the health checker tells the balancer to pull backend three from the pool, so traffic only flows to healthy nodes.
The insight: a load balancer is only as good as its health checks; the algorithm spreads load, but the gated pool is what hides failure.

optionA.text: Route to whichever backend has the fewest in-flight requests. It tracks real load, so a backend stuck on slow requests stops getting new ones until it drains — even load under variable durations.

Health checks are what detect the failure — the LB periodically probes each backend and drops unhealthy ones from rotation, so a crashed node stops receiving traffic. Without health checks, 1/N of requests keep erroring.

cdn-edge.proof: A cache-control decision function that classifies each response as edge-cacheable or not, plus an edge hit-ratio calculation over a request mix.
cdn-edge.unlock: You can decide what belongs at the edge, set the right Cache-Control, and estimate the origin offload a CDN provides.
cdn-edge.outcome: Push static and cacheable content to edge locations near users: understand Cache-Control (public/private, max-age, no-store), what is cacheable vs dynamic, and how edge hit ratio cuts origin load and latency.
cdn-edge.doNotClaim: Don't claim a CDN speeds up "everything" — only cacheable content is served from the edge; per-user dynamic responses must not be edge-cached.

cdn-edge.text: A team puts their whole site behind a CDN and users start seeing OTHER users' account pages, because a personalized, private response got cached at the edge and served to everyone. A CDN is powerful but blunt: it caches whatever Cache-Control tells it to, so the skill is deciding what is safely cacheable and marking dynamic/private responses no-store. This lesson makes cacheability a computed decision and quantifies the origin offload.

A CDN (content delivery network) is a fleet of edge caches spread geographically close to users. A request for cacheable content is served from the nearest edge — low latency, and the origin never sees it — while a miss is fetched from the origin and cached at the edge for the next user. What is cacheable is governed by the CACHE-CONTROL header: public (any cache may store it) vs private (only the user's browser); max-age (seconds it stays fresh); no-store (never cache — for sensitive or per-request data); no-cache (revalidate before use). STATIC assets (images, CSS, JS, videos) are ideal edge content: identical for everyone, long max-age. DYNAMIC, PERSONALIZED responses (a logged-in dashboard, a cart) must be private or no-store so one user's data is never served to another. The payoff is the EDGE HIT RATIO: the fraction of requests served from the edge, which directly offloads the origin and cuts latency.

cdn-edge.prompt: Before reading: which of these should be edge-cached with a long max-age, and which must be no-store — a site logo PNG, and a logged-in user's account balance page?
cdn-edge.reveal: The logo PNG: edge-cache it with a long max-age and public — it is identical for every user and changes rarely, so serving it from the edge is pure win. The account balance page: no-store (or at least private) — it is personalized and sensitive, so if the edge cached it, a different user could be served someone else's balance. The rule: cache what is shared and static; never edge-cache per-user or sensitive dynamic responses.

cdn-edge.intro: Decide cacheability from response attributes, then compute the edge hit ratio.
steps: Personalized or sensitive responses → no-store; never let them reach an edge cache.
Static, shared assets → public with a long max-age.
Shared-but-changing content → public with a short max-age.
Edge hit ratio = edge-served requests / total; it measures origin offload.
cdn-edge.commonMistake: Edge-caching a personalized or authenticated response (missing private/no-store). The CDN serves one user's cached page to the next user requesting that URL — a data leak. Per-user and sensitive responses must be marked no-store (or private) so only static/shared content lives at the edge.

cdn-edge.text: A CDN moves cacheable content to edge nodes physically near users, so a hit is served in a few milliseconds from a nearby city instead of a cross-continent round trip to the origin — and, just as importantly, the origin never processes that request, so its load drops by the edge hit ratio. What may be cached is dictated entirely by the CACHE-CONTROL response header, which is a contract between origin and caches: PUBLIC means any shared cache (including the CDN edge) may store the response; PRIVATE restricts it to the end user's own browser; MAX-AGE=N sets how many seconds it stays fresh before revalidation; NO-STORE forbids caching anywhere (for sensitive or strictly per-request data); NO-CACHE allows storage but requires revalidation before reuse. The classification that matters: STATIC, identical-for-everyone assets — images, CSS, JS bundles, video segments — are ideal edge content and get long max-age and public, because caching them once serves millions. DYNAMIC, PERSONALIZED responses — a logged-in dashboard, a shopping cart, anything tied to a user or a session — must be private or no-store, because an edge cache keyed by URL would otherwise serve one user's data to the next, a real and common security bug. The metric that justifies the CDN is the EDGE HIT RATIO: the fraction of requests answered at the edge; a high ratio means most traffic never touches the origin, which is both the latency win and the scaling win. So the craft is deciding, per response, whether it is shared-and-static (push it to the edge with a long life) or per-user-dynamic (keep it off the edge entirely), and then measuring the hit ratio to confirm the offload.
cdn-edge.title: The edge caches only what is shared; Cache-Control is the contract
Edge caching by Cache-Control
cdn-edge.subtitle: static goes to the edge; dynamic/private goes to origin

storyboard.say: A user's request never crosses the continent first — it lands at the nearest edge cache, a CDN node sitting in a city close to them.
The edge doesn't guess what's safe to keep — it reads the Cache-Control header, the contract the origin stamps on every response.
Static assets marked public get stored at the edge, so the next user in that city is served in milliseconds and the origin never hears about it.
On a miss, the edge fetches from the origin server once, caches the answer, and every later request for it stays local.
Personalized responses must say no-store — cache someone's account page at the edge and every user in that city sees it.
So private traffic always goes to origin, and the whole system rests on one header: Cache-Control decides what the edge may keep and what it must never touch.

cap-and-consistency.proof: A CP-vs-AP decision function that, per data requirement, chooses whether to sacrifice availability (stay consistent) or serve stale (stay available) during a partition.
cap-and-consistency.unlock: You can state, for a given piece of data, whether it must be CP or AP and defend it with the CAP theorem.
cap-and-consistency.outcome: Apply the CAP theorem: under a network partition you must choose Consistency OR Availability, and pick strong vs eventual consistency from what the data actually requires (PACELC extends this to the no-partition case).
cap-and-consistency.doNotClaim: Don't claim a system is "consistent AND available" during a partition — CAP proves you get at most one of those two when the network splits.

cap-and-consistency.text: During a network blip between data centers, a bank keeps serving account balances from both sides and a customer double-spends — because the design chose availability over consistency for data that needed the opposite. CAP is not a slide; it is the law that when the network partitions, you must PICK: refuse the request to stay consistent, or answer with possibly-stale data to stay available. This lesson turns that choice into a per-data decision you can defend.

The CAP theorem (Eric Brewer's 2000 conjecture, proven by Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch in 2002) states that a distributed data store cannot simultaneously guarantee all three of: CONSISTENCY (every read sees the most recent write), AVAILABILITY (every request gets a non-error response), and PARTITION TOLERANCE (it keeps working despite dropped messages between nodes). Since network partitions are a fact of life, partition tolerance is not optional — so the real choice under a partition is C vs A. A CP system refuses/ blocks requests it cannot serve consistently (banking, inventory); an AP system answers with possibly-stale data to stay up (feeds, likes, DNS). PACELC (Daniel Abadi, 2010) extends this: if Partitioned, choose A or C; Else (normal operation) choose Latency or C — because even without a partition, waiting for global consistency costs latency. CONSISTENCY MODELS name the spectrum: STRONG (linearizable — reads always see the latest write) vs EVENTUAL (replicas converge over time; reads may be stale).

cap-and-consistency.prompt: Before reading: during a partition, an inventory system for a limited-stock flash sale can either reject some purchases or risk overselling. Which does a correct design choose, and what is it giving up?
cap-and-consistency.reveal: It chooses CONSISTENCY (CP): reject or block purchases it cannot confirm against a single authoritative count, giving up AVAILABILITY for the duration of the partition. Overselling limited stock is a correctness violation you cannot undo cheaply, so you would rather serve fewer purchases than sell inventory that does not exist. By CAP, during the partition you cannot have both — and for scarce inventory, consistency wins over uptime.

cap-and-consistency.intro: Choose CP or AP per data requirement: correctness-critical → CP; availability-critical → AP.
steps: Partition tolerance is mandatory in a distributed store — the real choice is C vs A.
Correctness-critical data (money, inventory, uniqueness) → CP: refuse rather than diverge.
Availability-critical data (feeds, counts, presence) → AP: serve stale rather than fail.
PACELC reminds you that even without a partition, strong consistency costs latency.
cap-and-consistency.commonMistake: Declaring a whole system "consistent and highly available" as if CAP did not apply. Under a partition you get at most one of C or A; the honest design states, per data type, which one it sacrifices — and different data in the same system can make different choices.

cap-and-consistency.text: The CAP theorem — conjectured by Brewer (2000) and formally proven by Gilbert and Lynch (2002) — says a distributed data store cannot at once guarantee CONSISTENCY (every read returns the most recent write), AVAILABILITY (every request receives a non-error response), and PARTITION TOLERANCE (it keeps operating despite lost or delayed messages between nodes). Because real networks DO partition, partition tolerance is not something you can opt out of; therefore, at the moment of a partition, the design must choose between C and A. A CP choice keeps data correct by refusing or blocking any request it cannot serve consistently — the right call for money, inventory, and uniqueness constraints, where a wrong answer is worse than no answer. An AP choice keeps serving, returning possibly-stale data and reconciling later — the right call for feeds, like-counts, presence, and DNS, where being up matters more than being perfectly fresh. Crucially this is a PER-DATA decision, not a per-system one: the same application can make account balances CP and the activity feed AP. PACELC (Abadi, 2010) completes the picture: if there is a Partition, trade A vs C; Else, in normal operation, trade Latency vs Consistency — because a strongly consistent read may need to coordinate across replicas, which costs time even when nothing is broken. The consistency-model spectrum names your options: STRONG (linearizable) consistency guarantees every read sees the latest acknowledged write, at higher latency and lower availability; EVENTUAL consistency lets replicas diverge briefly and converge, buying latency and availability at the cost of possible staleness. Naming, per data, where you sit on that spectrum is what "designing for consistency" actually means.

storyboard.say: It starts with a network partition: the link between data centers drops, and both sides keep running without seeing each other's writes.
You cannot opt out of partitions — real networks fail. So the partition forces a decision you must have designed in advance.
That decision is CAP's real content: while partitioned, each piece of data gets consistency or availability — never both.
Choose CP and the system stays consistent: it blocks or rejects any request it can't answer correctly, trading uptime for truth.
Choose AP and the system stays available: every request gets an answer, even a stale one, and conflicts are reconciled later.
Money and inventory require CP — a bank serving balances from both sides of a partition is how a customer double-spends.
Feeds and likes require AP — a slightly stale like count is fine, but downtime isn't. The insight: choose C or A per data, not per system.
