async-queues.proof: An idempotent consumer with a dedup ledger that processes each message-id exactly once even when the same message is delivered multiple times.
async-queues.unlock: You can build a consumer that is safe under at-least-once delivery and explain why exactly-once is usually idempotency plus dedup.
async-queues.outcome: Decouple work with a message queue and handle its realities: at-least-once delivery means duplicates, so consumers must be IDEMPOTENT, and backpressure protects a slow consumer.
async-queues.doNotClaim: Don't claim a queue delivers "exactly once" — most give at-least-once, so duplicates are normal and your consumer must dedup them.

async-queues.text: A payment worker consumes a "charge card" message, the network hiccups before it acknowledges, the queue redelivers the message, and the customer gets charged TWICE. Queues decouple producers from consumers, but the delivery guarantee is almost always AT-LEAST-ONCE, which means duplicates are not an edge case — they are guaranteed. This lesson builds the idempotent consumer with a dedup ledger that makes redelivery harmless.

A message queue decouples a producer from a consumer: the producer enqueues work and returns immediately; a consumer processes it asynchronously, absorbing bursts and surviving consumer downtime. The delivery guarantee is the crux. AT-LEAST-ONCE (the common default) guarantees a message is delivered but may deliver it MORE than once — because acknowledgments can be lost, a consumer may process a message and crash before acking, so the queue redelivers it. AT-MOST-ONCE risks losing messages. True EXACTLY-ONCE processing is expensive and usually approximated as at-least-once delivery PLUS an idempotent consumer: the consumer records each processed message-id in a DEDUP LEDGER and skips any id it has already handled, so redelivery is a no-op. BACKPRESSURE handles a consumer that cannot keep up — the queue buffers, and the producer is slowed or shed rather than overwhelming the consumer. IDEMPOTENCY (processing the same message twice has the same effect as once) is the property that makes at-least-once safe.

async-queues.prompt: Before reading: your queue guarantees at-least-once delivery and a "send email" message is delivered twice. What must the consumer do so the user does not get two emails?
async-queues.reveal: The consumer must be IDEMPOTENT via a dedup ledger: before acting, it checks whether this message-id has already been processed; if so, it skips (the email was already sent) and just acknowledges. Only a never-seen id triggers the actual send, and the id is recorded so the inevitable redelivery is a no-op. At-least-once delivery makes duplicates certain, so exactly-once EFFECT comes from the consumer deduping, not from the queue.

async-queues.intro: An idempotent consumer: check the dedup ledger by message-id before doing the work.
steps: At-least-once delivery means the same message-id can arrive more than once.
Before performing the side effect, check the dedup ledger for the message-id.
If already present, skip — the effect already happened; just acknowledge.
If new, do the effect exactly once and record the id so redelivery is a no-op.
async-queues.commonMistake: Assuming the queue delivers exactly once and performing a side effect without deduping. Under at-least-once delivery a redelivered message runs the effect twice — a double charge, a duplicate email — so the consumer, not the queue, must guarantee exactly-once EFFECT via a dedup ledger.

async-queues.text: A message queue turns a synchronous, coupled call into an asynchronous, decoupled one: the producer enqueues and moves on, and a consumer processes the message later, which lets the system absorb bursts (the queue grows instead of failing) and survive consumer restarts (messages wait). The decisive property is the DELIVERY GUARANTEE. The overwhelmingly common one is AT-LEAST-ONCE: the queue will deliver a message, but may deliver it more than once, because the acknowledgment path is unreliable — a consumer can finish the work and then crash before its ack is recorded, so the queue, seeing no ack, redelivers. That makes DUPLICATES a certainty, not an anomaly. The disciplined response is not to wish for exactly-once delivery (which requires expensive coordination and still cannot cover external side effects) but to make the CONSUMER idempotent: give every message a stable id, keep a DEDUP LEDGER of processed ids, and, before performing the side effect, check the ledger — if the id is present, the work already happened, so skip and re-acknowledge; if it is new, perform the effect exactly once and record the id. This composition — at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer — delivers exactly-once EFFECT, which is what you actually care about (one charge, one email), and it is robust precisely because it assumes redelivery will happen. The other reality queues manage is BACKPRESSURE: when the consumer cannot keep up, the queue buffers the backlog and the system slows or sheds producers rather than crushing the consumer — the queue acting as a shock absorber between mismatched rates.

storyboard.say: A payment producer enqueues a charge-card message and returns immediately — the queue decouples it from whoever does the work.
The queue delivers the message to the consumer, but the guarantee is at-least-once: delivered for sure, possibly more than once.
If the consumer finishes the charge but crashes before its ack lands, the queue sees no ack and redelivers — a duplicate arrives.
So before doing anything, the consumer checks a dedup ledger: have I already seen this message id?
If the id is new, the ledger records it and the side effect runs exactly once — the card is charged a single time.
If the id is already recorded, the ledger says skip — redelivery becomes a harmless no-op, which is what idempotent means under at-least-once.

consensus-quorum.proof: A quorum validator that, given N/R/W, decides whether the configuration guarantees a read sees the latest acknowledged write (R + W > N).
consensus-quorum.unlock: You can tune (N, R, W) to trade consistency against latency/availability and prove when reads are guaranteed fresh.
consensus-quorum.outcome: Understand how replicas agree: leader election picks one coordinator, and a read/write quorum with R + W > N guarantees a read overlaps the latest write.
consensus-quorum.doNotClaim: Don't claim more replicas alone give consistency — consistency comes from the quorum overlap R + W > N, not from the replica count N.

consensus-quorum.text: A cluster with 5 replicas still returns stale reads, because it writes to 1 and reads from 1 — no overlap, so a read can miss the latest write entirely. Consistency in a replicated store is not about how many copies you have; it is about the QUORUM MATH: reads and writes must be guaranteed to overlap. This lesson makes R + W > N the checkable rule that decides whether a configuration is consistent.

When data is replicated across N nodes, the system must AGREE on the current value. Two mechanisms. LEADER ELECTION selects a single coordinator (via a consensus protocol like Raft/Paxos) so writes have one ordering authority, avoiding split-brain. QUORUMS let you tune consistency without a single leader for every operation: a write must be acknowledged by W of the N replicas, and a read must gather responses from R of the N. The guarantee is the OVERLAP condition R + W > N (from Amazon's Dynamo): if the read set and write set together exceed N, they must share at least one replica, so any read is guaranteed to include a replica holding the latest acknowledged write. Tuning the dial: high W (e.g. W=N) makes writes consistent but slow/less-available; high R makes reads consistent but slower; a common balanced choice is N=3, W=2, R=2 (sum 4 > 3), which survives one node failure while guaranteeing fresh reads.

consensus-quorum.prompt: Before reading: N=5 replicas, W=1 (write to one), R=1 (read from one). Can a read miss the latest write? What is the smallest R+W that fixes it?
consensus-quorum.reveal: Yes — with W=1, R=1 the write set and read set are single replicas that may be different nodes, so a read can hit a replica that never received the write (R+W = 2, which is NOT > 5). To guarantee overlap you need R + W > N, i.e. R + W ≥ 6 for N=5. For example W=3, R=3 (sum 6) forces the read and write quorums to share at least one replica, so every read includes the latest write. The replica count N alone guarantees nothing; the overlap does.

consensus-quorum.intro: Check the quorum overlap: a read is guaranteed fresh iff R + W > N.
steps: A write must be acked by W replicas; a read must gather R replica responses.
R + W > N forces the read and write sets to overlap in at least one replica.
That shared replica holds the latest acknowledged write, so the read sees it.
Tune the dial: higher W/R buys consistency at the cost of latency/availability.
consensus-quorum.commonMistake: Believing that adding replicas (raising N) improves consistency. Raising N without raising R and W actually makes overlap HARDER (R + W must exceed a larger N). Consistency comes from the R + W > N relationship, not from the replica count.

consensus-quorum.text: Replicating data across N nodes creates the agreement problem: which value is current? Two tools solve it. LEADER ELECTION uses a consensus protocol (Raft, Paxos) to choose exactly one coordinator that orders writes, preventing split-brain where two nodes both think they are in charge and diverge. QUORUM replication offers a tunable alternative: instead of routing every operation through one leader, you require a write to be acknowledged by W of the N replicas and a read to collect responses from R of the N. The load-bearing rule, from Amazon's Dynamo, is the overlap condition R + W > N. The intuition is pigeonhole: if the set of W replicas that stored the write and the set of R replicas answering the read together number more than N, they cannot be disjoint — they must share at least one replica, and that replica holds the most recent acknowledged write, so the read is guaranteed to observe it. This turns "is my system consistent?" into arithmetic. It also exposes the tuning dial: to make writes strongly consistent you push W up (at W = N a write must reach every replica — maximally consistent, but one slow or down replica blocks all writes); to make reads consistent you push R up (slower reads); and the sweet spot for many systems is N = 3 with W = 2, R = 2, whose sum 4 exceeds 3 so reads are guaranteed fresh, while tolerating a single replica failure on either path. The critical misconception to kill is that more replicas means more consistency — raising N alone widens the gap R + W must clear, so it is the RELATIONSHIP among N, R, and W, not the size of N, that determines whether a read can ever be stale.

storyboard.say: Five copies of your data does not mean fresh reads — what matters is whether the write set and the read set are guaranteed to share a replica.
A write goes out and waits for acknowledgments from W replicas — here it lands on replica 1 and replica 2 before it is confirmed.
Replica 3 never received the write — it still holds the old value, and that is completely normal in a quorum system.
Later, a read fans out to R replicas — it happens to query replica 2 and the stale replica 3.
Because R plus W exceeds N, pigeonhole math forces at least one shared replica — here replica 2 sits in both the write set and the read set.
Replica 2 holds the latest version, so the read compares responses and returns the fresh value — replica 3's stale copy is outvoted.
That is the whole guarantee: choose W and R so the sets must overlap, and every read is certain to touch a replica carrying the newest write.

R=1, W=1 sums to 2, not greater than 3, so the read and write sets can be disjoint and a read can miss the latest write — regardless of how large N is.

distributed-fallacies.doNotClaim: Don't claim a remote call is "just like a local call" — the fallacies are exactly the assumptions that make distributed systems fail in ways local code never does.

distributed-fallacies.text: A design assumes a remote service call always returns quickly and never fails, so it has no timeout and no retry — and the first time the network hiccups, threads pile up waiting forever and the whole service hangs. The eight FALLACIES OF DISTRIBUTED COMPUTING are the exact false assumptions behind failures like this. This lesson makes them a checklist you run against a design to catch the assumption before it causes the outage.

The fallacies of distributed computing are a canonical list of false assumptions that engineers coming from single-machine code make when building distributed systems. Most were articulated by L. Peter Deutsch and colleagues at Sun Microsystems, with the eighth added by James Gosling. They are: (1) the network is reliable, (2) latency is zero, (3) bandwidth is infinite, (4) the network is secure, (5) topology does not change, (6) there is one administrator, (7) transport cost is zero, (8) the network is homogeneous. Each names an assumption that is safe locally but false across a network, and each maps to a real defense: assume the network fails → add timeouts, retries, and idempotency; assume latency is nonzero → batch and cache; assume bandwidth is finite → paginate and compress. Underlying them is PARTIAL FAILURE — in a distributed system some parts fail while others keep running, so you cannot treat the whole as up-or-down — and unsynchronized CLOCKS, which is why you cannot trust wall-clock ordering across machines.

distributed-fallacies.prompt: Before reading: a service calls a remote API with no timeout and no retry, and stores a timestamp from the remote machine's clock to order events. Which fallacies is it committing?
distributed-fallacies.reveal: At least three. No timeout/retry assumes "the network is reliable" (fallacy 1) and implicitly "latency is zero" (fallacy 2) — a call can hang or fail, so unbounded waiting piles up. Trusting a remote machine's clock to order events assumes clocks are synchronized, which relates to the fallacies' clock/consistency assumptions — different machines' clocks drift, so wall-clock timestamps cannot reliably order distributed events. The fix: bounded timeouts + retries + idempotency, and logical/causal ordering instead of raw wall-clock time.

distributed-fallacies.commonMistake: Treating a remote call like a local function call — synchronous, instant, and infallible. That single mental error is the root of most of the eight fallacies: it drops timeouts (reliability), ignores round-trip cost (latency), and assumes the call always succeeds (partial failure).

distributed-fallacies.text: The fallacies of distributed computing are the industry's checklist of the false assumptions programmers carry over from single-machine code, most articulated by L. Peter Deutsch and colleagues at Sun Microsystems (the eighth added by James Gosling). They are, in order: (1) THE NETWORK IS RELIABLE — it is not; packets drop, connections reset, so every remote call needs a timeout, retries, and idempotency. (2) LATENCY IS ZERO — every round trip costs real milliseconds, so chatty fine-grained calls are lethal; batch and cache. (3) BANDWIDTH IS INFINITE — it is finite, so unbounded payloads and missing pagination will saturate a link; compress and page. (4) THE NETWORK IS SECURE — assume hostile networks and encrypt in transit. (5) TOPOLOGY DOESN'T CHANGE — nodes come and go and IPs move, so hardcoded hosts break; use service discovery. (6) THERE IS ONE ADMINISTRATOR — real systems span teams and clouds with different policies. (7) TRANSPORT COST IS ZERO — moving bytes costs money and CPU (serialization, egress). (8) THE NETWORK IS HOMOGENEOUS — links and nodes differ, so uniform assumptions fail. Two deeper truths sit beneath the list. PARTIAL FAILURE: unlike a single machine that is up or down, a distributed system has some parts failing while others run, so "did it work?" is often genuinely unknown (the ambiguous timeout) and must be handled with idempotent retries and reconciliation. And CLOCKS: separate machines' clocks drift, so you cannot order events across them by wall-clock time — you need logical/causal ordering. Running a design against these eight named assumptions turns "distributed systems are hard" into a concrete audit that catches the missing timeout or the hardcoded host before it becomes an incident.

storyboard.say: It starts with a design under review — code that calls a remote service and quietly assumes the network will behave like a local function call.
We run the design through a fallacy audit, checking each of the classic false assumptions engineers carry over from single-machine code.
First flag: the design trusts the network is reliable — there is no timeout and no retry, so one dropped packet leaves threads waiting forever.
Second flag: it assumes latency is zero, making chatty fine-grained calls where every round trip silently adds real milliseconds.
Third flag: hosts are hardcoded, assuming the topology never changes — the moment a server moves or scales, the design breaks.
Each flagged assumption maps to a concrete defense: timeouts and retries for reliability, batching and caching for latency, service discovery for topology.
That is the insight: the fallacies are not trivia — they are an audit checklist where every unstated assumption you catch becomes a specific fix you ship.

failure-modes-blast-radius.proof: A blast-radius propagator that, given a dependency graph, computes every component that fails when one component goes down — and shows how a bulkhead shrinks it.
failure-modes-blast-radius.unlock: You can compute the blast radius of any component and place bulkheads to contain cascading failures.
failure-modes-blast-radius.outcome: Trace how one component's failure propagates through its dependents (the blast radius), and use bulkheads to contain it so a single failure does not take down the whole system.
failure-modes-blast-radius.doNotClaim: Don't claim a component failure is "isolated" without tracing its dependents — one shared dependency can cascade a local failure into a total outage.

failure-modes-blast-radius.text: A single recommendation service goes down, and because the product page calls it synchronously with no isolation, the whole product page fails — then the homepage that embeds it fails — and a minor dependency has taken down the site. This is a BLAST RADIUS problem: failures propagate through the dependency graph. This lesson computes that radius from the graph and shows how a bulkhead contains it.

In a system of interdependent components, a failure rarely stays local: everything that DEPENDS on the failed component can fail too, and their dependents in turn — the set of everything that goes down is the BLAST RADIUS. You compute it by walking the dependency graph from the failed node to all its (transitive) dependents. The defense is a BULKHEAD (from ship design: watertight compartments so one breach does not sink the vessel): isolate components so a failure in one cannot spread — separate thread pools/connection pools per dependency, so a slow dependency exhausts only its own pool; graceful degradation, so a caller treats a failed non-critical dependency as optional and returns a reduced result instead of failing. A bulkhead effectively CUTS an edge in the propagation graph, shrinking the blast radius from "the whole system" to "one feature."

failure-modes-blast-radius.prompt: Before reading: the product page calls recommendations synchronously and fails if recommendations fails. The homepage embeds the product page. If recommendations goes down, what is the blast radius? How does a bulkhead change it?
failure-modes-blast-radius.reveal: Blast radius = recommendations → product page → homepage: all three fail, because each hard-depends on the one below. A bulkhead breaks the chain by making recommendations OPTIONAL to the product page — the product page catches the recommendation failure and renders without that section (graceful degradation). Now the blast radius is just recommendations; the product page and homepage stay up with a reduced experience. The bulkhead cut the propagation edge.

failure-modes-blast-radius.commonMistake: Calling every dependency synchronously and hard-failing if any is unavailable, with no isolation. A single non-critical service then becomes a single point of failure for everything upstream — the blast radius is the whole system when it should have been one feature.

failure-modes-blast-radius.text: A production system is a graph of components that depend on one another, and the crucial reliability insight is that failure is TRANSITIVE: when a component fails, everything that hard-depends on it can fail, and everything that depends on THOSE can fail, and so on. The BLAST RADIUS of a failure is the full set of components that go down as a result — you compute it by traversing the dependency graph from the failed node outward to all its transitive dependents. A design where a minor service (recommendations, avatars, related-items) is called synchronously and treated as required means its blast radius includes every page that embeds it, up to the whole site — a tiny failure with a system-sized radius. The containment tool is the BULKHEAD, named for a ship's watertight compartments: you isolate components so a breach in one cannot flood the rest. Concretely that means (a) separate resource pools per dependency — its own thread pool and connection pool — so a slow or failing dependency exhausts only its own resources and cannot starve the caller's threads and hang everything; and (b) graceful degradation — the caller treats a non-critical dependency as OPTIONAL, catches its failure, and returns a reduced result (the product page without the recommendation strip) instead of failing outright. In graph terms, a bulkhead REMOVES the propagation edge from the caller to the failed dependency, so the blast radius shrinks from "everything upstream" to just the failed component. Designing for reliability is therefore two moves: compute the blast radius of each critical component to find the dangerous single points, and place bulkheads on the edges that would otherwise cascade a local failure into a global one.

failure-modes-blast-radius.subtitle: a failure propagates to dependents unless an edge is cut

storyboard.say: Start with the recommendations service — a minor dependency — and it has just gone down.
The product page calls it synchronously and treats it as required, so when recs fails, the product page fails with it.
Failure is transitive: the homepage embeds the product page, so it goes down too — the whole site dies from one small service.
That set of everything knocked out — recs, product page, homepage — is the blast radius: walk the graph from the failure to all its dependents.
The fix is a bulkhead: declare recommendations optional and isolate the failure so it cannot propagate past that edge.
With recs walled off, the bulkhead serves a degraded product page — no recommendations, but the page and homepage stay up.
The insight: blast radius is set by your edges, not your failures — cut the synchronous hard dependency and a tiny outage stays tiny.

resilience-patterns.doNotClaim: Don't claim retries make a system resilient — retrying a hard-down dependency amplifies the outage; you need a breaker to stop.

resilience-patterns.text: A dependency goes down and the caller retries every failed request three times, so the dependency now gets 3× the traffic while it is trying to recover — the retries are a self-inflicted denial-of-service. Resilience is not "retry harder"; it is a small set of composed patterns: bound the wait (timeout), retry transient failures gently (backoff), and STOP calling a dead dependency (circuit breaker). This lesson builds the breaker state machine that makes the caller give up fast and probe for recovery.

Three patterns protect a caller from a flaky dependency. TIMEOUT bounds how long you wait — without it, one stuck call holds a thread forever (the hang from the fallacies lesson). RETRY WITH EXPONENTIAL BACKOFF handles TRANSIENT failures (a blip, a brief 503) by retrying after growing delays (e.g. 100ms, 200ms, 400ms), ideally with jitter to avoid synchronized retry storms — but only for idempotent operations and only a few times. The CIRCUIT BREAKER (Michael Nygard, Release It!) handles a dependency that is DOWN, not just blipping: it is a state machine. CLOSED = normal, calls pass, failures are counted; when failures exceed a threshold it trips to OPEN = calls fail fast immediately without touching the dependency, sparing it and the caller; after a cooldown it moves to HALF-OPEN = a single trial call is allowed — if it succeeds the breaker CLOSES (recovered), if it fails it re-OPENS. Together: timeout bounds each attempt, backoff spaces retries, and the breaker stops retrying entirely once the dependency is clearly down.

resilience-patterns.prompt: Before reading: a circuit breaker is OPEN after a dependency failed repeatedly. The cooldown elapses. What happens on the next call, and what are the two possible outcomes?
resilience-patterns.reveal: After the cooldown the breaker moves to HALF-OPEN and allows a single TRIAL call through to test the dependency. Two outcomes: if the trial SUCCEEDS, the dependency has recovered, so the breaker transitions to CLOSED and normal traffic resumes; if the trial FAILS, the dependency is still down, so the breaker returns to OPEN and starts another cooldown. Half-open is the controlled probe that lets the breaker detect recovery without flooding a still-broken dependency with full traffic.

resilience-patterns.intro: The circuit breaker state machine: count failures to open, cooldown to half-open, trial to close.
steps: CLOSED: calls pass; count consecutive failures; at the threshold, trip to OPEN.
OPEN: fail fast; after the cooldown elapses, allow the next call as a HALF-OPEN probe.
HALF-OPEN: one trial call — success → CLOSED (reset), failure → OPEN (new cooldown).
Compose with timeout (bound each call) and backoff (space retries while closed).
resilience-patterns.commonMistake: Retrying a hard-down dependency aggressively with no circuit breaker. The retries multiply load on a service that is already failing, delaying its recovery and amplifying the outage — you need a breaker to STOP calling once the dependency is clearly down.

resilience-patterns.text: Resilience against a flaky dependency is three composed patterns, each solving a different failure shape. A TIMEOUT bounds a single call: because "the network is reliable" is a fallacy, any call can stall, and without a deadline one stuck request holds a thread indefinitely and cascades into a hang — so every remote call gets a timeout and fails fast when exceeded. RETRY WITH EXPONENTIAL BACKOFF handles TRANSIENT faults — a momentary blip, a brief overload — by retrying after exponentially growing delays (100ms, 200ms, 400ms…), preferably with random JITTER so many clients do not retry in lockstep and create a synchronized thundering herd; retries must be limited in number and only applied to idempotent operations. But retries are exactly wrong when the dependency is not blipping but DOWN — then every retry piles more load on a service trying to recover, turning a partial outage into a self-inflicted denial of service. The CIRCUIT BREAKER (from Michael Nygard's Release It!, popularized by Martin Fowler) fixes that with a three-state machine wrapping the call. CLOSED is normal operation: calls pass through and consecutive failures are counted; when the count crosses a threshold the breaker TRIPS to OPEN. OPEN means the dependency is presumed dead: calls FAIL FAST immediately without even attempting the dependency, which protects both the caller (no waiting) and the dependency (no load) — and after a cooldown timeout the breaker moves to HALF-OPEN. HALF-OPEN allows a single TRIAL call: if it succeeds the dependency has recovered and the breaker returns to CLOSED (resetting the failure count); if it fails the breaker snaps back to OPEN for another cooldown. Composed, these three give a caller that waits bounded time per attempt, retries gently through transient faults, and stops entirely once a dependency is genuinely down — probing periodically to detect its recovery.

storyboard.say: The breaker starts CLOSED: every request flows to the dependency, and each failure is quietly counted against a threshold.
When failures cross the threshold, the breaker trips to OPEN — instead of retrying harder, it stops calling entirely and fails fast.
OPEN is the protection: with zero traffic hitting it, the struggling dependency finally gets room to recover instead of a retry storm.
After a cooldown elapses, the breaker moves to HALF-OPEN and lets a single probe request through as a careful test.
That one trial call decides everything: if it succeeds, the breaker closes and normal traffic resumes.
If the trial fails, the breaker re-opens and waits out another cooldown — never flooding a dependency that is still down.
The insight: resilience is not retrying harder — the breaker converts repeated failure into fast failure, so your client stops being the attack.

After the cooldown it goes HALF-OPEN and lets a single trial call through — success closes the breaker (recovered), failure re-opens it. It neither queues nor blocks forever; it probes.

observability-slos.proof: An error-budget calculator that turns an SLO and a measurement window into allowed downtime, budget consumed, and a burn rate that flags when the budget will be exhausted early.
observability-slos.unlock: You can turn a reliability goal into an SLO, an error budget, and a burn-rate alert.
observability-slos.outcome: Make reliability measurable: define an SLI (a metric), set an SLO (a target), derive the error budget (1 − SLO), and compute the burn rate that tells you whether you are spending the budget too fast.
observability-slos.doNotClaim: Don't claim a service is "reliable" without an SLI and an SLO — reliability you cannot measure is an opinion, and the error budget is what makes it a decision.

observability-slos.text: Leadership asks "is the service reliable?" and gets a shrug and a gut feeling. Then an incident burns through a month of acceptable downtime in a single afternoon and nobody notices until customers complain. Reliability has to be a NUMBER: an SLI you measure, an SLO you target, an error budget you spend, and a burn rate that alarms when you are spending it too fast. This lesson turns reliability into that arithmetic.

Google's SRE practice makes reliability quantitative with three linked terms. An SLI (service level INDICATOR) is a measured metric of service health — request success rate, latency under a threshold, availability. An SLO (service level OBJECTIVE) is the TARGET for an SLI over a window — "99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days." The ERROR BUDGET is the flip side: 1 − SLO, the amount of failure you are ALLOWED. A 99.9% SLO permits 0.1% failure, which over 30 days is about 43 minutes of downtime — that budget is a resource you spend on risk (deploys, experiments). The BURN RATE measures how fast you are consuming it: burning at 1× exactly exhausts the budget over the window; burning at 10× exhausts a month's budget in ~3 days, which should page someone. The discipline: if the budget is healthy, ship faster; if it is nearly spent, freeze risky changes until reliability recovers.

observability-slos.prompt: Before reading: your SLO is 99.9% success over 30 days. Roughly how much total downtime does the error budget allow, and what does a 99.9% target imply about acceptable failures?
observability-slos.reveal: 99.9% success means 0.1% allowed failure. Over 30 days (≈ 43,200 minutes) that is about 43.2 minutes of allowed downtime/failure — the error budget. The 99.9% target explicitly ACCEPTS that ~0.1% of requests may fail; chasing 100% is infinitely expensive and pointless, so the budget is a deliberate allowance you spend on shipping and experiments. When it is nearly gone you slow down; when it is healthy you can take more risk.

observability-slos.intro: From SLO and window to allowed downtime, budget consumed, and burn rate.
steps: Error budget (minutes) = (1 − SLO) × window minutes — the failure you are allowed.
Burn rate = (actual bad fraction of time) ÷ (allowed bad fraction of time).
Burn rate 1× spends the budget exactly over the window; >1× spends it too fast.
A high burn rate (e.g. ≥ 10×) is an early warning to freeze risky changes and alert.
observability-slos.commonMistake: Setting a 100% availability target (or none at all). 100% is unachievable and infinitely expensive, and having no SLO means no error budget — so there is no principled way to decide when to ship versus when to stop and fix reliability. Pick an achievable SLO and manage its budget.

observability-slos.text: Observability makes a system's behavior inspectable through metrics, logs, and traces; Site Reliability Engineering turns that into decisions with three linked definitions. An SLI, the service level INDICATOR, is a concrete measured signal of health — the fraction of successful requests, the fraction served under a latency threshold, availability. An SLO, the service level OBJECTIVE, is a target for that indicator over a defined window: "99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days." The pivotal reframe is the ERROR BUDGET, which is simply 1 − SLO: the amount of unreliability you have explicitly decided to ALLOW. A 99.9% SLO permits 0.1% failure, which over a 30-day window is roughly 43 minutes of downtime — and that is not a threat, it is a BUDGET, a resource you deliberately spend on the risk of shipping features, running experiments, and doing migrations. From it comes the BURN RATE: the ratio of how fast you are actually consuming the budget to the rate that would spend it exactly over the window. A burn rate of 1× exhausts the budget precisely at the end of the window; a burn rate of 10× means you are consuming a month's allowance in about three days, which should page an engineer because at that pace an incident is eating the whole budget in an afternoon. This is what makes reliability a decision rather than a feeling: when the error budget is healthy, the team can ship aggressively; when it is nearly spent or burning fast, risky changes freeze until reliability recovers. And the deeper point the error budget encodes is that 100% reliability is the wrong target — it is infinitely expensive and blocks all progress — so you choose an achievable SLO and then manage its budget as the shared currency between shipping speed and reliability.

storyboard.say: Start with what you can actually measure: the SLI, a concrete signal of health like the fraction of requests that succeed.

Every failed request spends that budget, and the burn rate tells you how fast: an afternoon incident can torch a whole month's allowance.
The burn rate is a decision, not a dashboard: burning slow means budget to spare, so ship faster and take risks.
Burning hot means the budget is nearly gone, so freeze risky changes until it recovers; reliability is now a number you spend, not a gut feeling.

rate-limiting-load-shedding.proof: A token-bucket rate limiter that refills at a steady rate, allows bursts up to capacity, and admits or rejects each request based on available tokens.
rate-limiting-load-shedding.unlock: You can size a token bucket for a rate and burst, and explain how load shedding preserves the core under overload.
rate-limiting-load-shedding.outcome: Protect a service from overload: implement a token-bucket rate limiter (rate + burst) and understand graceful load shedding — dropping or degrading low-priority work to keep the core serving.
rate-limiting-load-shedding.doNotClaim: Don't claim a rate limiter just "caps requests" — a token bucket separates sustained rate from burst allowance, and load shedding chooses WHAT to drop.

rate-limiting-load-shedding.text: A traffic spike or a misbehaving client hammers your API, and with no rate limit the service tips over — taking down every user, not just the abusive one. Rate limiting is the valve that admits a sustained rate while tolerating short bursts, and load shedding is the triage that drops low-priority work first so the core survives. This lesson builds the token-bucket limiter that makes both precise.

Two mechanisms keep a service alive under more load than it can handle. RATE LIMITING caps how much a client (or the whole system) may do. The TOKEN BUCKET is the standard algorithm: a bucket holds up to CAPACITY tokens and refills at a steady REFILL RATE (tokens/sec); each request costs one token — if a token is available the request is admitted and a token is removed, otherwise it is rejected (or throttled). This elegantly separates two concerns: the refill rate bounds the SUSTAINED average, while the capacity bounds the BURST (a full bucket lets that many requests through instantly). Contrast the leaky bucket, which shapes output to a constant rate with no burst. LOAD SHEDDING is what you do when even the allowed load exceeds capacity: rather than degrade uniformly (everyone slow) or crash (everyone down), you DROP or degrade the lowest-priority work first — shed background/optional requests, serve cached/reduced responses — so the critical path keeps working. Both are graceful-degradation tools: fail some requests deliberately to keep the system serving the rest.

rate-limiting-load-shedding.prompt: Before reading: a token bucket has capacity 10 and refills 2 tokens/sec. It starts full. 10 requests arrive instantly, then 4 more one second later. How many are admitted?
rate-limiting-load-shedding.reveal: First burst: the bucket starts full with 10 tokens, so all 10 instant requests are admitted (bucket now empty). One second later the bucket has refilled 2 tokens (2 tokens/sec × 1s). Of the 4 new requests, 2 are admitted (using both tokens) and 2 are rejected. Total: 12 admitted, 2 rejected. The capacity (10) set the burst size; the refill rate (2/sec) set the sustained rate — exactly the two knobs a token bucket separates.

rate-limiting-load-shedding.intro: A token bucket: refill by elapsed time (capped at capacity), spend one token per admitted request.
steps: The bucket starts full and refills lazily by elapsed time × refill rate, capped at capacity.
Capacity bounds the BURST; refill rate bounds the SUSTAINED average.
Each admitted request spends one token; an empty bucket rejects (or throttles).
Load shedding decides WHAT to drop when even allowed load exceeds capacity — lowest priority first.
rate-limiting-load-shedding.commonMistake: Conflating rate and burst — using one fixed limit per interval (a fixed window). A fixed window allows a full quota at the boundary AND another full quota just after, so two windows' worth can arrive back-to-back. The token bucket cleanly separates sustained rate (refill) from burst (capacity), avoiding that boundary spike.

rate-limiting-load-shedding.text: A service has finite capacity, and two mechanisms keep it from being destroyed by more demand than it can serve. RATE LIMITING throttles how fast requests are admitted, and the TOKEN BUCKET is the workhorse algorithm because it captures two distinct limits with one structure. Picture a bucket that holds up to CAPACITY tokens and is refilled at a constant REFILL RATE of r tokens per second; every request must take one token to proceed, and if the bucket is empty the request is rejected or delayed. The refill rate r governs the SUSTAINED throughput — over the long run you cannot exceed r requests/sec, because that is how fast tokens arrive. The capacity b governs the BURST — a bucket that has sat idle is full, so up to b requests can be admitted in an instant before the rate limit bites. That separation is exactly what real APIs want ("100 requests/sec sustained, but tolerate a burst of 100"), and it is why the token bucket is preferred over a fixed-window counter (which allows a full quota on each side of a window boundary, permitting a 2× spike) and over the leaky bucket (which enforces a smooth constant output and permits no burst at all). When demand exceeds even the rate-limited capacity — a genuine overload — the answer is LOAD SHEDDING: instead of letting everything slow down together or crash, the system deliberately drops or degrades the LOWEST-priority work first (background jobs, optional enrichment, non-logged-in traffic) and protects the critical path, and it may serve cached or reduced responses to survive. Both are forms of graceful degradation: you choose to fail some requests on purpose so the system keeps serving the rest, rather than failing all of them by accident.
rate-limiting-load-shedding.title: The token bucket separates rate from burst; shedding chooses what to drop
Token bucket + load shedding
rate-limiting-load-shedding.subtitle: refill sets sustained rate, capacity sets burst; overload sheds low priority

storyboard.say: Requests arrive at whatever rate clients feel like sending, but your service can only survive a finite rate, so every request first hits the token bucket.
Meanwhile a refill process drips tokens into the bucket at r per second; that steady drip is the sustained rate you are willing to serve long-term.
The bucket holds at most capacity tokens, so a quiet period banks up to b tokens; that stored slack is exactly how big a burst you can absorb at once.
Every request must withdraw one token, so admission reduces to a single question: is there a token in the bucket right now?
If a token is there, the request takes it and gets served; within budget, users never notice the limiter exists.
If the bucket is empty you are past both budgets, so the request is rejected — and under overload you shed low-priority work first to protect what matters.
One bucket encodes two limits: refill rate caps sustained throughput, capacity caps the burst, and shedding turns overload into triage instead of collapse.

optionB.text: Shape output to a constant 100/sec, queuing or dropping anything above it. Perfectly smooth downstream load and no bursts — good for protecting a fragile downstream, but it forbids the burst you wanted to allow.
optionB.label: Leaky bucket

rate-limiting-load-shedding.guidance: Use the token bucket (A) when you want a sustained rate WITH burst tolerance — the common case for public APIs. Use the leaky bucket (B) when the downstream must see a perfectly smooth rate and bursts would harm it. The deciding question is whether bursts are desirable (token) or dangerous (leaky).
rate-limiting-load-shedding.question: Your API needs 100 req/sec sustained but should tolerate short bursts. Token bucket or leaky bucket?

options: Both control the same thing — together they just set one overall cap on the total number of requests allowed.
Refill rate sets the sustained long-run rate; capacity sets the maximum burst that a full bucket admits at once.
Neither one affects bursts; a token bucket smooths all traffic to a constant rate and forbids bursts entirely.
Refill rate sets the burst size, while capacity governs the per-request latency each admitted request experiences.
rate-limiting-load-shedding.question: In a token bucket, what do the refill rate and the capacity control, respectively?
rate-limiting-load-shedding.explanation: The refill rate (tokens/sec) bounds the long-term SUSTAINED rate, because that is how fast tokens replenish. The capacity bounds the BURST, because a full bucket lets that many requests through instantly. Separating these two knobs is exactly why the token bucket is preferred over a single fixed-window limit.

tradeoff-analysis-adrs.proof: A tradeoff scorer that ranks design options against weighted criteria and produces the decision an ADR would record.
tradeoff-analysis-adrs.unlock: You can turn a fuzzy "which architecture?" argument into a scored decision with recorded rejected alternatives.
tradeoff-analysis-adrs.outcome: Make and record architectural decisions deliberately: score options against weighted criteria, know when NOT to distribute (a monolith often wins), and capture the decision + rejected alternatives in an ADR.
tradeoff-analysis-adrs.doNotClaim: Don't claim the "best" architecture in the abstract — the best option is the highest weighted score against THIS system's criteria, and it is often the simplest.

tradeoff-analysis-adrs.text: A team spends weeks debating microservices vs monolith by trading opinions, then splits into 12 services and drowns in distributed-systems complexity for a product with 500 users — a decision no one wrote down or scored. Architecture is a series of tradeoffs, and the senior skill is making them EXPLICIT: weight the criteria, score the options, pick the winner, and record it (with the rejected alternatives) in an ADR. This lesson turns architecture arguments into a defensible calculation.

An architect's core output is DECISIONS under conflicting constraints, and two disciplines keep them honest. TRADEOFF ANALYSIS: enumerate the real options, define the criteria that matter for THIS system (e.g. simplicity, scalability, team velocity, operational cost), WEIGHT them by importance, score each option per criterion, and pick the highest weighted total — which forces the conversation onto explicit priorities instead of preferences. A recurring result is "do NOT distribute": a MONOLITH is simpler to build, deploy, debug, and reason about, and for most systems (small team, moderate scale) it beats microservices, whose independent scaling and deployment come at the cost of network calls, distributed data, and operational overhead you should only pay when scale or org size demands it. The ARCHITECTURE DECISION RECORD (ADR) captures each significant decision as a short document: the context, the decision, the alternatives considered and WHY they were rejected, and the consequences — so future engineers understand the reasoning rather than re-litigating it.

tradeoff-analysis-adrs.prompt: Before reading: a 3-person team building a new product with a few hundred users is choosing between a monolith and 10 microservices. Which usually wins, and what criterion decides it?
tradeoff-analysis-adrs.reveal: The MONOLITH usually wins for a small team at low scale. The deciding criteria are SIMPLICITY and TEAM VELOCITY: a monolith is one deploy, one codebase, in-process calls, and easy local debugging, so a small team ships far faster and operates far less. Microservices buy independent scaling and deployment — valuable at large scale or with many teams — but at that size they impose distributed-systems overhead (network failure, data consistency, ops) that a 3-person team cannot afford. You distribute when scale or org structure FORCES it, not by default.

tradeoff-analysis-adrs.intro: Score options against weighted criteria; the highest weighted total is the recorded decision.
steps: Enumerate real options (monolith, modular monolith, microservices).
Define and WEIGHT the criteria that matter for this system.

Record the chosen option AND the rejected alternatives (with scores) in an ADR.
tradeoff-analysis-adrs.commonMistake: Choosing microservices by default ("that's how scalable systems are built") without weighing simplicity and team size. For most systems the distributed-systems tax — network failure, data consistency, deployment orchestration — outweighs the scaling benefit you do not yet need; the monolith is frequently the correct, boring answer.

tradeoff-analysis-adrs.text: Architecture is the practice of making decisions under conflicting constraints, and its two disciplines are scoring the tradeoff and recording it. TRADEOFF ANALYSIS replaces "I prefer X" with a weighted decision matrix: list the genuine options, name the criteria that actually matter for THIS system and its stage — simplicity, scalability, team velocity, operational cost, time-to-market — assign each criterion a WEIGHT reflecting its importance here (a pre-product-market-fit startup weights velocity and simplicity heavily; a hyperscale platform weights scalability), score every option against every criterion, and choose the highest weighted total. The value is not the arithmetic precision but that it forces the argument onto explicit priorities: disagreements become disagreements about weights, which are discussable, instead of clashing intuitions. A result this method surfaces again and again is WHEN NOT TO DISTRIBUTE. A monolith — one codebase, one deployment, in-process calls, transactional local data, trivial local debugging — is dramatically simpler than a set of microservices, and simplicity is a first-class virtue. Microservices buy independent scaling, independent deployment, and team autonomy, but they impose the entire distributed-systems tax this course has been about: network calls that fail, data split across services with no cross-service transaction, and heavy operational machinery. You should pay that tax only when SCALE or ORGANIZATION size genuinely forces it, not because microservices sound modern. Finally, every significant decision is captured in an ARCHITECTURE DECISION RECORD: a short, dated document stating the context, the decision, the alternatives considered and precisely why each was rejected, and the consequences accepted. The ADR is what lets a future engineer understand why the system is the way it is — and prevents the team from re-fighting a settled decision because no one remembered the reasoning.

the-interview-method.unlock: You can run a design discussion end-to-end with a method, and catch when you skipped a step.
the-interview-method.outcome: Drive a system-design discussion with a repeatable method: frame requirements → estimate → high-level design → deep-dive a component → find the bottleneck → discuss tradeoffs — and check your process is complete.
the-interview-method.doNotClaim: Don't claim you "designed the system" if you jumped to boxes — a complete design walks frame → estimate → high-level → deep-dive → bottleneck → tradeoff.

the-interview-method.text: In a design interview a candidate immediately starts drawing databases and caches, never asks a requirement, never estimates scale, and never identifies the bottleneck — and produces an impressive-looking diagram that answers no actual question. The difference between senior and junior here is METHOD: a repeatable sequence that guarantees you frame before you build and find the bottleneck before you optimize. This lesson makes that method a checklist you can verify you followed.

Whether in an interview or a real design doc, strong system design follows a repeatable METHOD rather than improvisation. The six steps: (1) FRAME — clarify functional and non-functional requirements and constraints (the first lesson's skill); (2) ESTIMATE — back-of-envelope the scale (RPS, storage, bandwidth) so the design is sized to reality; (3) HIGH-LEVEL DESIGN — sketch the major components and the request path (the building blocks); (4) DEEP-DIVE — pick one component and detail it (the data model, the cache strategy, the sharding); (5) BOTTLENECK — identify where this design will break FIRST under the estimated load and address it; (6) TRADEOFFS — state what you optimized for and what you gave up (consistency vs availability, cost vs latency). Running these in order is what separates a designed system from a pile of boxes: you frame before building, size before choosing, and find the bottleneck before optimizing the wrong thing.

the-interview-method.prompt: Before reading: a candidate opens a design interview by drawing "client → API → database → cache." What crucial steps did they skip, and why does it matter?
the-interview-method.reveal: They skipped FRAME (no requirements — what does it do, at what scale, how consistent?) and ESTIMATE (no RPS/storage numbers). It matters because the architecture is DERIVED from requirements and scale: without them, the boxes are ungrounded guesses that might be wildly over- or under-built. They also have not identified the BOTTLENECK, so they cannot know whether the cache even addresses the real constraint. A diagram without frame, estimate, and bottleneck answers no actual question.

the-interview-method.intro: The six-step method and a checker that verifies all steps were walked in order.
steps: Frame requirements and constraints FIRST — never start with boxes.
Estimate scale so the design is sized to real numbers.
Sketch the high-level components, then deep-dive one.
Find the bottleneck before optimizing, then state the tradeoffs you accepted.
the-interview-method.commonMistake: Jumping straight to the high-level design (drawing components) and skipping frame + estimate. Without requirements and scale numbers, you cannot justify a single component or know where the bottleneck is — you have produced a diagram, not a design, and it usually answers the wrong question.

the-interview-method.text: System design done well is a repeatable PROCESS, and the process is what distinguishes a senior answer from a junior one — juniors draw a familiar diagram; seniors run a method that guarantees the diagram answers the actual question. The six steps, in order: FRAME the problem by clarifying functional requirements, non-functional requirements (scale, latency, availability, consistency), and constraints — because everything downstream is derived from these. ESTIMATE the scale with back-of-the-envelope math (peak RPS, storage/year, bandwidth) so every subsequent choice is sized to reality rather than taste. Produce a HIGH-LEVEL DESIGN: the major components and the request path, at the altitude of boxes and arrows. Then DEEP-DIVE into one component that matters — the data model and its sharding key, the cache strategy and its invalidation, the consistency mechanism — showing you can go from the map to the mechanism. Identify the BOTTLENECK: given the estimated load, where does THIS design saturate first (the single database? the hot key? the synchronous fan-out?), and address it specifically — this is the step that separates real engineering from box-drawing, because optimizing anything else is wasted. Finally, state the TRADEOFFS: what you optimized for and what you consciously gave up (you chose availability over strong consistency for the feed; you chose a cache and accepted staleness), because a design without acknowledged tradeoffs is hiding its weaknesses. Running these in sequence is the point: framing before building prevents solving the wrong problem, estimating before choosing prevents mis-sizing, and finding the bottleneck before optimizing prevents polishing a component that was never the constraint. The method is also self-checking — you can literally verify you walked all six steps and catch the one you skipped.

designing-a-real-system.proof: A composed shortener with a requirements ledger, capacity budget, request/data-flow diagram, unique codes, coherent shard routing, cache behavior, rate limits, failure probes, and exact invariant checks.
designing-a-real-system.unlock: You can compose the course's primitives into one coherent system and verify it behaves correctly.
designing-a-real-system.outcome: Apply the whole ladder to one end-to-end design — a URL shortener — composing id generation, caching, sharding, and rate limiting into a working request path and verifying its invariants.
designing-a-real-system.doNotClaim: Don't claim the pieces work because each passed alone — a real system is proven by the invariants that hold when they COMPOSE.

designing-a-real-system.text: Every prior lesson built one primitive: estimation, caching, sharding, rate limiting, consistency. A real system is not any one of them — it is all of them COMPOSED on one request path, and the proof it works is the INVARIANTS that hold across the composition: every short code is unique, every redirect resolves, load spreads across shards, and creation is rate-limited. This lesson designs a URL shortener end-to-end and verifies those invariants with computed checks.

A URL shortener is the canonical end-to-end design because it exercises the whole ladder in a small space. CREATE: take a long URL, generate a UNIQUE short code (a base-62 encoding of a monotonic id, or a hashed id), and store the mapping. REDIRECT (the hot path, read-heavy): look up the code and 301/302 to the long URL — served from a CACHE for speed, falling back to the sharded store on a miss. SCALE: the mapping table is SHARDED by short code (consistent hashing) so writes and storage spread across nodes; the redirect cache absorbs the read majority. PROTECT: creation is RATE-LIMITED (token bucket) so no client can exhaust the id space or hammer the store. The design's correctness is defined by INVARIANTS: (1) uniqueness — no two long URLs get the same code; (2) resolvability — every created code redirects to its URL; (3) balanced sharding — codes spread across shards; (4) rate-limited creation — bursts beyond capacity are rejected. Composing the primitives and checking these invariants is what "designing a real system" means.

designing-a-real-system.prompt: Before reading: for a URL shortener, which primitives from this course does the CREATE path need, and which does the REDIRECT path need?
designing-a-real-system.reveal: CREATE needs: unique id/code generation (uniqueness invariant), a sharded store to spread writes (sharding), and a rate limiter to bound creation (token bucket). REDIRECT needs: a cache for the hot read path (caching/hit rate), with a fallback to the sharded store on a miss (sharding), and it is the read-heavy path so it dominates the capacity estimate. The two paths compose the estimation, caching, sharding, and rate-limiting lessons into one system — which is exactly what makes the shortener the canonical end-to-end exercise.

designing-a-real-system.intro: Compose id-gen, sharding, cache, and rate limiting into one shortener and verify its invariants.
steps: Generate a unique code by base-62 encoding a monotonic id — uniqueness by construction.
Shard the mapping by code so writes and storage spread across nodes.
Serve redirects from a cache; fall back to the sharded store on a miss.
Rate-limit creation with a token bucket; verify every invariant holds after composing.
designing-a-real-system.commonMistake: Testing each primitive in isolation and assuming the system works. The real bugs live in the composition — a redirect that the cache serves but the shard never stored, or a code collision under concurrent creation — so correctness must be proven by the system-level INVARIANTS, not by each part passing alone.

designing-a-real-system.text: Designing a real system is the act of COMPOSING the primitives the course built into one coherent request path, and its correctness is defined not by the parts but by the INVARIANTS that must hold across the whole. Take the URL shortener. Its CREATE path generates a short code and stores a mapping; the natural technique is to encode a monotonically increasing id in base-62 (0-9, a-z, A-Z), which yields short, URL-safe codes that are UNIQUE by construction because each id is used once — this satisfies the uniqueness invariant without a collision check. The mapping is SHARDED by short code (via consistent hashing) so that as the system grows, writes and storage distribute across nodes rather than piling on one — the balanced-sharding invariant. Its REDIRECT path is the hot, read-heavy path: a lookup of code → long URL, served from a CACHE so the overwhelming read majority never touches the store, with a fallback to the correct shard on a miss — and the resolvability invariant demands that every code ever created still redirects to its URL, whether from cache or store. Creation is RATE-LIMITED with a token bucket so no client can flood the creation path or race the id generator — the rate-limited-creation invariant. The crucial mindset shift at this level is that verifying each primitive alone is NOT verifying the system: the interesting failures are compositional — a cache that returns a value the shard never persisted, a code that two concurrent creates both claim, a redirect to a shard the router computed differently than the writer did. So the proof of a real design is a set of computed, system-level checks: create some URLs and assert all codes are unique; redirect each and assert every one resolves to the right URL; count codes per shard and assert they spread; and fire a creation burst past the limiter and assert the excess is rejected. When those invariants hold across the composed path, you have designed a system — not assembled boxes.

storyboard.say: One client, two request paths: writing a new short link, and the read-heavy redirect that serves every click after it.
Creates hit the rate limiter first, so a burst of write traffic can never starve the system or mint codes faster than it can store them.
Admitted creates take a monotonic id, encode it in base sixty-two, and store the mapping — each id is used once, so uniqueness holds by construction.
The mapping lands in a store sharded by short code with consistent hashing, so writes and storage spread across nodes as the system grows.
Redirects are the hot path: the client hits the cache, and on a hit we answer straight away with a 301 to the long URL.
On a miss, the cache falls back to the owning shard, fills itself, and still resolves — slower, but never wrong, because the store is the source of truth.
The design is the composition: limiter, id generator, shards, and cache each solve one problem, and the invariants — unique codes, correct redirects — hold across all of them.

optionA.text: Encode an ever-increasing id. Codes are unique by construction (no collision check needed) and compact, but they are sequential — guessable and they leak how many links exist.
optionA.label: Monotonic counter → base-62

optionB.text: Generate random codes and check the store for collisions before committing. Unguessable and non-sequential, but you must handle (rare) collisions with a retry and pay a lookup per create.
optionB.label: Random string + collision check

designing-a-real-system.guidance: Use the counter (A) when uniqueness-by-construction and compactness matter and enumeration is acceptable (or you obscure the counter with an encoding/offset). Use random codes (B) when guessability is a real concern (private links) and accept the collision-check cost. Both satisfy the uniqueness invariant; choose by whether enumeration is a threat.

options: Invariants are just a formality; a thorough suite of unit tests on each individual primitive already proves the system.
Interesting bugs are compositional — a reader and writer sharding by different keys — caught only by whole-path invariants.
Primitives never contain bugs once they have been written, so the only place a real defect can hide is in the glue code between them.
A system genuinely cannot be tested at all until it is deployed, so invariants are the only check available beforehand.
designing-a-real-system.question: Why is a composed system verified by system-level invariants rather than by each primitive passing in isolation?
designing-a-real-system.explanation: Each primitive can be individually correct while their COMPOSITION is broken — a code stored on one shard but looked up on another, a cache serving a value the store never had. Only invariants over the whole path (uniqueness, resolvability, balanced sharding, rate-limited creation) catch these compositional failures, which is why they define the design's correctness.

capstone-design-and-defend.text: Given a spec — a read-heavy news feed at high scale with a mix of correctness-critical and availability-tolerant data — you must produce a design AND prove it holds up: that its capacity estimate fits the infrastructure budget, that its store choices match each data type's consistency needs, that its cache clears the hit-rate target the read-heavy load requires, and that a single component failure is contained. This capstone is the whole course as one graded, computed defense — no vibes, only checks.

The capstone is the entire ladder applied and DEFENDED. You take a written spec (traffic, data types, budget, availability target) and produce a design, then subject it to GATES that are each a computed check derived from an earlier lesson: (1) CAPACITY — the estimated peak RPS and storage (back-of-envelope) must fit within the provisioned budget (servers × per-server capacity), or the design is under-provisioned. (2) CONSISTENCY — each data type must be assigned a store/model matching its needs: correctness-critical data gets a CP/quorum store, availability-tolerant data gets an AP/eventual store (CAP). (3) CACHE — for a read-heavy workload the cache hit rate must clear a target (e.g. ≥ 0.8) so the origin is not overwhelmed (caching). (4) FAILURE CONTAINMENT — a designated non-critical component's failure must have a bounded blast radius (bulkheads), not a system-wide one. A design PASSES only when every gate's computed check passes; that is what "design and defend" means — the defense is arithmetic, not assertion.

capstone-design-and-defend.prompt: Before reading: you claim a design is "scalable and reliable." What four computed checks would actually PROVE that, drawing on this course?
capstone-design-and-defend.reveal: Four gates: (1) CAPACITY — computed peak RPS and storage fit the provisioned budget (estimation). (2) CONSISTENCY — each data type is on a store whose model matches it: CP for correctness-critical, AP for availability-tolerant (CAP). (3) CACHE — the hit rate meets the read-heavy target so the origin is protected (caching). (4) CONTAINMENT — a non-critical component's failure has a bounded blast radius (bulkheads). "Scalable and reliable" is proven when all four computed checks pass — not when the diagram looks impressive.

capstone-design-and-defend.intro: Run every gate as a computed check; the design passes only if all pass.
steps: Capacity gate: provisioned RPS ≥ peak RPS AND storage budget ≥ storage needed.
Consistency gate: every correctness-critical type on CP, every tolerant type on AP.
Cache gate: the cache hit rate meets the read-heavy target.
Containment gate: the non-critical component's blast radius is within the allowed bound.
capstone-design-and-defend.commonMistake: Defending a design with narrative ("we use Kafka, so it scales") instead of computed checks. Scalability and reliability are properties you PROVE against the spec's numbers — capacity fits, consistency matches, cache clears its target, failure is contained — and a design that cannot pass those computed gates is not done, however good the story sounds.

capstone-design-and-defend.text: The capstone crystallizes the course's founding principle — proof, not vibes — into a design you must DEFEND with arithmetic. You start from a spec: the traffic (DAU, actions, peak factor), the data types and their consistency needs, the infrastructure budget, and the availability/hit-rate targets. You produce a design: the stores, the cache, the sharding, the failure isolation. Then you subject that design to a series of GATES, each a computed check inherited directly from an earlier lesson, and the design is valid only if ALL of them pass. The CAPACITY gate takes the back-of-envelope peak RPS and storage estimate and checks they fit the provisioned budget (servers × per-server RPS, storage budget) — an under-provisioned design fails here regardless of how elegant it is. The CONSISTENCY gate walks each data type and verifies it sits on a store whose model matches its nature: correctness-critical data (money, inventory) on a CP/quorum store, availability-tolerant data (feeds, counts) on an AP/eventual store — a mismatch (a bank balance on an AP store, or a like-count needlessly CP) fails the gate. The CACHE gate confirms the cache hit rate clears the target the read-heavy workload demands, so the origin is not overwhelmed. The CONTAINMENT gate confirms that a designated non-critical component's failure has a blast radius within the allowed bound — i.e. that bulkheads actually isolate it. This is the essence of staff-level design: you do not argue that a system is scalable and reliable, you DERIVE it — every claim is a computed check against a requirement, and a design that cannot pass all four gates is, by definition, not finished. Composing the whole course this way is the final proof that you can not only design a system but defend that it meets its spec.

storyboard.say: Everything starts with the spec: traffic numbers, data types, budget, and availability targets — plus the design you built to meet them.
First, the capacity gate: your back-of-envelope peak RPS and storage must fit the provisioned budget — servers times per-server capacity.
Pass capacity and the consistency gate takes over: every data type must land in a store whose guarantees match its correctness needs.
Next, the cache gate: your hit-rate math must show the read-heavy load actually stays off the backing stores at peak.
Then containment: when a shard or dependency fails, the blast radius must stay bounded — the design survives partial failure by arithmetic, not hope.
Notice the gates are chained with AND — one failed check anywhere invalidates the whole design; there is no partial credit.
Only when all four computed checks pass does the design earn its verdict — that's the course's founding principle: proof, not vibes.
